statement: Section 70104 of the 2025 reconciliation law raises the per-child credit in section 24(h) from $2,000 to $2,200, removes the end-of-2025 expiry, and applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024.
anchor:
SEC. 70104. EXTENSION AND ENHANCEMENT OF INCREASED CHILD TAX
CREDIT.

(a) Extension and Increase of Expanded Child Tax Credit.--Section
24(h) is amended--

(1) in paragraph (1), by striking ``, and before January 1,
2026'',

(2) in paragraph (2), by striking ``$2,000'' and inserting
``$2,200'', and

shall apply to taxable years beginning after December
31, 2024.
context: Primary law: P.L. 119-21, signed July 4, 2025 (second Trump administration). Striking the end date makes the TCJA credit design permanent: there is no sunset.

statement: Section 70104 of the 2025 reconciliation law sets the refundable limit per child at $1,400 as increased by the cost-of-living adjustment for taxable years after 2024, and increases the $2,200 credit amount by the cost-of-living adjustment for taxable years after 2025, rounding any increase down to a multiple of $100.

subsection (h)(5) shall be increased

In the
case of a taxable year beginning after 2025, the $2,200 amount
in subsection (h)(2) shall be increased

If any increase under this subsection is
not a multiple of $100, such increase shall be rounded to the

context: Primary law. The new section 24(i) indexes only these two dollar amounts; the $2,500 earnings floor and the $200,000/$400,000 phase-out thresholds (EV-SEC-006, EV-SEC-007) are not indexed in the text.

statement: For taxable years beginning in 2026, the IRS sets the maximum child tax credit at $2,200 and the amount used to determine the refundable portion at $1,700 per child.
anchor:
For taxable years beginning in 2026, the
maximum amount of the credit allowed under § 24(a) is $2,200.

the amount used in
§ 24(d)(1)(A) to determine the amount of the credit under § 24 that may be refundable is
$1,700.
context: IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32 (second Trump administration), applying statutory indexing. The 2026 refundable limit equals the 2025 figure of $1,700 (EV-SEC-004), so the $2,200 credit is not indexed upward for 2026 either: the cost-of-living adjustment rounds down to the next multiple of $100.

statement: CRS describes the maximum additional child tax credit (the refundable portion) as $1,700 per child for 2025, adjusted for inflation, and says the 2025 law makes the TCJA credit changes permanent and sets the credit at $2,200 per child, adjusted for inflation.
anchor: the maximum ACTC at $1,700 per child (2025 figure, adjusted for inflation)
This provision makes permanent the TJCA's changes to the credit and permanently raises the maximum credit to $2,200 per child (adjusted for inflation).
context: CRS (nonpartisan) description of enacted law, P.L. 119-21. Matches the statute (EV-SEC-001, EV-SEC-002). The source text spells TCJA as "TJCA" in this sentence.

statement: From taxable year 2025, no child tax credit is allowed unless the return includes the Social Security number of the taxpayer (of at least one spouse on a joint return) and of the qualifying child, each issued to a U.S. citizen or under the listed Social Security Act provisions and before the return's due date.
anchor:
No credit shall be allowed under
this section to a taxpayer with respect to any
qualifying child unless the taxpayer includes on the
return of tax for the taxable year--

the taxpayer's social security number
(or, in the case of a joint return, the social
security number of at least 1 spouse), and

the social security number of such
qualifying child.

to a citizen of the United States or
pursuant to subclause (I)
before the due date for such return.
context: Primary law, section 70104(b), replacing section 24(h)(7). Before the law only the child needed an SSN; the new rule excludes citizen children with SSNs whose parents have only ITINs. Existing register entry on the same rule: EV-HOU-405 (from IRS Schedule 8812 instructions).

statement: The refundable part of the child tax credit is 15 percent of earned income above $2,500: the code applies 15 percent to earnings above $3,000 and then substitutes $2,500 for $3,000.
anchor: (i) 15 percent of so much of the taxpayer's earned income (within the meaning of section 32) which is taken into account in computing taxable income for the taxable year as exceeds $3,000, or
Subsection (d)(1)(B)(i) shall be applied by substituting "$2,500" for "$3,000".
context: U.S. Code, 2024 edition (before P.L. 119-21). Section 70104 amends section 24(h)(1) to remove the end date, so section 24(h)(6) stays in force with no end date; it does not amend section 24(d). The credit is therefore zero for a family with no income tax liability and under $2,500 of earnings (see EV-SEC-011).

statement: The child tax credit phases out by $50 for each $1,000 of modified adjusted gross income above $400,000 for a joint return and $200,000 for any other return.
anchor: reduced (but not below zero) by $50 for each $1,000 (or fraction thereof) by which the taxpayer's modified adjusted gross income exceeds the threshold amount.
the threshold amount shall be $400,000 in the case of a joint return ($200,000 in any other case).
context: U.S. Code, 2024 edition. Permanence rests on section 70104(a), which strikes the end date in section 24(h)(1); CRS R48611 (EV-SEC-004 source) states it: "increased the income limits to $200,000 for single filers and $400,000 for married couples filing jointly". The $50 per $1,000 is a 5 percent phase-out rate.

statement: CRS says the TCJA created a $500 nonrefundable credit, not adjusted for inflation, for dependents who are not qualifying children, and that the 2025 law makes the TCJA changes permanent.
anchor: created a $500 nonrefundable credit (not adjusted for inflation) for dependents who are not qualifying children
This provision makes permanent the TJCA's changes to the credit
context: CRS description of enacted law. Statute: section 24(h)(4)(A) (U.S. Code 2024 edition, SRC-3607). The credit is the only credit open to a child with an ITIN rather than an SSN (CBPP, SRC-3635, says so); a citizen child of parents with only ITINs may be claimed for it as a dependent.

statement: Section 70204 creates Trump accounts (new section 530A) and a Trump Accounts Contribution Pilot Program under which an election by the parent treats an eligible child as paying $1,000 of tax, which is refunded to the child's Trump account, for a qualifying child born after December 31, 2024 and before January 1, 2029.
anchor: SEC. 70204. TRUMP ACCOUNTS AND CONTRIBUTION PILOT PROGRAM.
Sec. 530A. Trump accounts.

TRUMP ACCOUNTS CONTRIBUTION
PILOT PROGRAM.

such eligible child shall be treated as making a payment
against the tax imposed by subtitle A (for the taxable year for which
the election was made) in an amount equal to $1,000.

who is born after December 31, 2024, and before
January 1, 2029,
context: Primary law. CRS (R48611, SRC-3011) adds that the beneficiary must be a U.S. citizen with a work-authorized SSN and that the account invests in a diversified U.S. stock index fund; contributions are capped at $5,000 a year. The $1,000 is a one-time deposit, not income support to the family.

statement: The 2025 law creates a deduction of $6,000 for each taxpayer age 65 or older for 2025 through 2028, reduced by 6 percent of modified adjusted gross income above $75,000 ($150,000 on a joint return), for taxpayers with work-eligible Social Security numbers.
anchor: It also temporarily creates a new $6,000 deduction for taxpayers (and their spouses, if married filing jointly) who are age 65 or older, from 2025 through 2028.
This amount is reduced by 6% of a taxpayer's modified adjusted gross income above $75,000 ($150,000 for those married filing jointly).
context: CRS description of enacted law (section 70103). Temporary: it ends after tax year 2028, before the January 2029 baseline date for the new administration. It is a deduction, so it is worth nothing to a household that owes no income tax.

statement: The Tax Policy Center estimated that in 2025, 17 million children under 17, one in four, would receive less than the full child tax credit because their parents earn too little; about 2 million get nothing because they earn under $2,500 and owe no tax.
anchor: But in 2025, the Tax Policy Center estimates that 17 million children under the age of 17—or one in four—will receive less than the full value of the credit because their parents earn too little.
Families that do not owe federal income taxes and earn less than $2,500 receive no CTC. That’s about 2 million children
locator: opening paragraphs; section on who receives the full value
context: Tax Policy Center (Urban-Brookings, nonpartisan), December 10, 2024: microsimulation for 2025 under the then-current $2,000 credit, before the 2025 law. The 17 million is the share below the $2,000 maximum; the later TPC post (EV-SEC-012) says the same count at $2,200.

statement: In June 2026 the Tax Policy Center restated that roughly 17 million children live in families that do not receive the full $2,200 per child because their families' earnings are too low.
anchor: roughly 17 million children live in families that do not receive the full $2,200 per child CTC because their families’ earnings are too low
context: Tax Policy Center (nonpartisan), June 10, 2026; written in reply to a second Trump administration Treasury analysis that stressed how many families receive the credit. The count differs from Columbia's 19 million (EV-SEC-013) in method: Columbia adds about two million moderate-income children newly short of a larger maximum.

statement: Columbia's Center on Poverty and Social Policy estimated that in 2025 more than 1 in 4 children (28%) under age 17, 19 million, would be ineligible for the full child tax credit under the 2025 law because family income is not high enough; a two-parent, two-child family needs at least $41,500.
anchor: more than 1 in 4 children (28%) under age 17 will be ineligible for the full Child Tax Credit under OBBBA because their family income is not high enough to qualify

This represents 19 million children left behind: 17 million children previously ineligible for the full credit who see no gains under OBBBA and remain ineligible for the full credit plus roughly two million children in moderate-income families newly ineligible for the full credit.
a two-parent family with two children will need a minimum of $41,500 in income to be eligible for the full credit under OBBBA
context: Columbia University Center on Poverty and Social Policy, August 6, 2025, brief by Collyer, Yera, Curran, Harris and Wimer; simulation on Census survey data of the law as signed; the center advocates a more fully refundable credit. Higher than TPC's 17 million (EV-SEC-012) because it counts the children whose families fall short of the larger $2,200 maximum.

statement: CBPP estimates that 19 million children, more than 1 in 4 children under 17, will receive less than the full $2,200 credit in 2026, or no credit, because their families earn too little, including half of Black children.
anchor: an estimated 19 million children — or more than 1 in 4 children under 17 — will receive less than the full $2,200 credit in 2026, or no credit at all, because their families earn too little
This includes half of Black children
context: Center on Budget and Policy Priorities (progressive-leaning; advocates expanding refundability), January 6, 2026, relying on Tax Policy Center estimates. Same count as Columbia (EV-SEC-013), so not independent of it in method.

statement: As reported by the Tax Policy Center in May 2025, the Joint Committee on Taxation estimated that approximately 2 million children with SSNs would be denied the child tax credit under the House bill's requirement that each adult taxpayer have an SSN.
anchor: the Joint Committee on Taxation estimates that approximately 2 million children with SSNs would be denied the CTC
locator: paragraph beginning "The House bill would change that"
context: Tax Policy Center (nonpartisan) quoting JCT (Congress's official nonpartisan scorer), May 29, 2025, about the House-passed bill; that bill required every adult on a joint return to hold an SSN, stricter than the enacted rule (one spouse suffices). JCT's estimate for the enacted text was not found. TPC repeated the 2 million in June 2026 (SRC-3632).

statement: The Bipartisan Policy Center, citing the Tax Policy Center, said 500,000 children who would otherwise be eligible could lose the credit under the enacted rule if no parent can produce an SSN.
anchor: The Tax Policy Center estimated that 500,000 children who would otherwise be considered eligible could lose access to the credit if no parent can produce an SSN to comply with the new requirement.
locator: section "The Impact of the New CTC Provisions on Families"
context: Bipartisan Policy Center (nonpartisan think tank), 2025, secondhand from a Tax Policy Center estimate that was not located at the source. Applies to the enacted one-parent-SSN rule, so it is far below the 2 million for the House bill (EV-SEC-015). Treat the range, 0.5 to 2 million, as unsettled.

statement: Tax Policy Center says the reconciliation law disallows the credit for U.S. citizen children who do not have at least one parent holding a Social Security number, and that Joint Committee on Taxation estimated around 2 million such children would lose it under a slightly stricter rule.
anchor: disallowing the credit for US citizen children if they do not have at least one parent who holds a Social Security number (SSN)
around 2 million US citizen children would lose the CTC under slightly more restrictive, but similar, Social Security number (SSN) requirements than those ultimately enacted
context: Tax Policy Center (nonpartisan), June 10, 2026, corrected June 11 to say "at least one parent". Describes the enacted rule correctly; the estimate is for the earlier, stricter text.

statement: A worker without a qualifying child must be at least age 25 but under age 65 at the end of the year to claim the earned income credit (for a joint return, at least one spouse must meet the age rule).
anchor: You must be at least age 25 but under age 65 at the end of the year. If married and filing a joint return, at least one spouse must meet the age rule.
context: IRS page last reviewed 2026-11-10 (second Trump administration). Statute: 26 U.S.C. 32(c)(1)(A)(ii)(II) (SRC-3608). The participation rate for the credit is in EV-HOU-399 (78 percent of eligible taxpayers, tax year 2021).

statement: Section 10102 of the 2025 reconciliation law limits the SNAP work-requirement exceptions to people under 18 or over 65, the medically unfit, parents or household members responsible for a child under 14, pregnant women, and American Indians, so a parent is excepted only while the child is under 14.
anchor:
SEC. 10102. MODIFICATIONS TO SNAP WORK REQUIREMENTS FOR ABLE-
BODIED ADULTS.
(A) under 18, or over 65, years of age;
(F) an Indian or an Urban Indian
context: Primary law. Previously the time limit applied to ages 18 to 54 without dependents. The consequences (ages 55 to 64 without children, and parents of children 14 or older, are covered) follow from the exceptions; CRS (EV-SEC-029) states them. Effective on enactment subject to USDA implementation guidance (CRS).

statement: CRS describes the enacted SNAP time limit as covering ages 18-64 and adults whose youngest child dependent is age 14 or older, and says the law strikes the exemptions for veterans, people experiencing homelessness and some people who aged out of foster care, and the sunset date.
anchor: The enacted bill expands the population subject to the time limit to ages 18-64 and adults whose youngest child dependent is age 14 or older. The proposal strikes the exemptions for veterans, individuals experiencing homelessness, and certain individuals who aged out of foster care, as well as the sunset date.
context: CRS (nonpartisan) description of enacted law. The ABAWD time limit is three months of benefits in a 36-month period unless the person works or trains 80 hours a month (CBO, EV-SEC-031).

statement: Section 10105 sets a state share of SNAP benefit costs from fiscal year 2028, by payment error rate: 0 percent below 6, 5 percent from 6 to under 8, 10 percent from 8 to under 10, and 15 percent at 10 percent or more.

A state whose 2025 (2026) error rate times 1.5 is 20 percent or more starts in fiscal year 2029 (2030). This delays but does not remove the cost share.

statement: Section 10106 cuts the federal share of SNAP state administrative costs from 50 percent through fiscal year 2026 to 25 percent for fiscal year 2027 and each year after.

statement: CBO estimated that the Thrifty Food Plan provision lowers the average monthly SNAP benefit from 2027, to $213 in 2034 against $227 in its January 2025 baseline, with no effect on participation.
anchor: CBO estimates that beginning in 2027, the average monthly benefit will be smaller
by 2034 that benefit will be $213 compared with $227 in the baseline projection for that year.
CBO does not expect that section 10101 will affect participation.
context: CBO (nonpartisan), August 11, 2025, relative to its January 2025 baseline; projection, each section as if implemented on its own. Text read through a full-text fetch.

statement: CRS reports that CBO estimated the Thrifty Food Plan change would reduce the average monthly SNAP benefit by $14 by 2034, and that the nutrition subtitle of the 2025 reconciliation law would reduce federal spending by almost $187 billion over 10 years (FY2025-FY2034).
anchor: The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimated that the Nutrition subtitle of P.L. 119-21 would reduce federal spending by almost $187 billion over 10 years (FY2025-FY2034)
By 2034, the policy change is estimated to reduce the average monthly benefit by $14.
locator: Summary; section on CBO participation and benefit estimates
context: CRS (nonpartisan) summarizing CBO. The task brief expected about $186 billion; CRS says "almost $187 billion". It is the nutrition subtitle in total (SNAP plus TEFAP grant), not SNAP alone.

statement: CBO estimated that the SNAP work-requirement changes reduce participation by roughly 2.4 million people in an average month over 2025-2034, including about 800,000 able-bodied adults through age 64 without dependent children and 300,000 adults 18 to 64 living with a child 14 or older.
anchor: CBO estimates that together those provisions will reduce participation in SNAP by roughly 2.4 million people in an average month over the 2025-2034 period.

Of those people, about 800,000 will be able-bodied adults through age 64 who do not live with dependent children. Another 300,000 will be able-bodied adults ages 18 to 64 who live with children who are age 14 or older.
context: CBO (nonpartisan), August 11, 2025, projection relative to the January 2025 baseline; each section as if implemented alone. CBO also expected about 1 million adults to lose waivers they would have had and a net 300,000 loss for veterans, homeless and former foster youth. CRS R48755 (EV-SEC-037) repeats it. Actual 2026 participation fell faster (EV-SEC-039, EV-SEC-040).

statement: CRS reports that CBO estimated the SNAP work provision reduces federal SNAP outlays by $69 billion over the 10-year window and reduces SNAP participation by roughly 2.4 million people in an average month.

reduce SNAP participation by roughly 2.4 million people in an average month

statement: Herd and Moynihan's 2018 book Administrative Burden argues that administrative burdens are the result of deliberate policy choices, not unintended byproducts, and cites Social Security as a program whose administrators minimized burdens for beneficiaries, with a take-up rate of about 100 percent.
anchor: are not simply unintended byproducts of governance, but the result of deliberate policy choices
the take-up rate is about 100 percent because the Social Security Administration keeps track of peoples’ earnings for them, automatically calculates benefits and eligibility
context: Russell Sage Foundation's summary of a 2018 book by Pamela Herd and Donald Moynihan (Georgetown); winner of the 2019 Louis Brownlow Book Award. The page is the publisher's description, not the book's text, and the about-100-percent take-up claim is the publisher's wording of the authors' argument. The book is a conceptual framework with case studies (United States, 1930s to 2010s), not a causal estimate.

statement: Currie's 2004 review of U.S. and U.K. research concludes that take-up of social benefits is raised by automatic or default enrollment and lowered by administrative barriers, and that removing individual barriers may have little effect, so the whole bundle of barriers must be addressed.
anchor: take up is enhanced by automatic or default enrollment and lowered by administrative barriers, although removing individual barriers does not necessarily have much effect, suggesting that one must address the whole bundle
context: Janet Currie (Princeton), NBER Working Paper 10488, May 2004; published as a chapter in Auerbach, Card and Quigley (eds.), Poverty, the Distribution of Income, and Public Policy (Russell Sage, 2006). A literature review, not a new estimate; it covers U.S. and U.K. programs (Medicaid, EITC, food stamps and others). Her 'default enrollment' conclusion is a reading of observational and quasi-experimental studies.

statement: In an IRS field experiment, mailings sent to 35,050 tax filers who had failed to claim $26 million of EITC benefits produced substantial additional claiming through the mere receipt of the mailing, simplification and the heightened salience of benefits, while attempts to reduce perceived stigma, application costs and audits did not.
anchor: experimental mailings distributed to 35,050 tax filers who failed to claim $26 million despite an initial notice

While the mere receipt of the mailing, simplification, and the heightened salience of benefits led to substantial additional claiming, attempts to reduce perceived costs of stigma, application, and audits did not.
context: Bhargava (Carnegie Mellon) and Manoli (UT Austin), American Economic Review 105(11), 2015. Randomized field experiment run with the IRS on filers who had received a first notice (tax year 2008 filers, per the paper); effects are on people who already file a return and were missing the credit, so it does not speak to non-filers. Peer reviewed.

statement: In a randomized experiment with 30,000 elderly people likely eligible for but not enrolled in SNAP, 6 percent of the control group enrolled over the next 9 months, compared with 11 percent of those given information only and 18 percent of those given information plus help applying.
anchor: 30,000 elderly individuals not enrolled in – but likely eligible for – the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)
Only 6 percent of the control group enrolls in SNAP over the next 9 months, compared to 11 percent of the Information Only group and 18 percent of the Information Plus Assistance group.
context: Amy Finkelstein (MIT) and Matthew Notowidigdo (Northwestern), NBER Working Paper 24652 (2018), published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics 134(3), 2019; funded by the Sloan Foundation; partner Benefits Data Trust. RCT among elderly people in Pennsylvania (BDT's service area); the effect applies to older adults and an assisted application, not to a general population.

statement: In the same SNAP experiment, people who enrolled in response to either intervention received lower benefits and were less sick than the average enrollee in the control group, which the authors read as evidence that frictions are greater for needier individuals.
anchor: The individuals who apply or enroll in response to either intervention receive lower benefits and are less sick than the average enrollee in the control group.
consistent with the existence of optimization frictions that are greater for needier individuals
context: Same RCT as EV-SEC-103 (shared authors, so not independent of it). It qualifies the take-up result: outreach that raises enrollment can still miss the neediest, which argues for automatic delivery over outreach and application help.

statement: In San Francisco SNAP data, cases assigned later-in-the-month recertification interview dates, which leave less time to reschedule missed interviews, were over 20 percent less likely to recertify; those that failed because of the later date lost an average of $600 in benefits the next year, and one quarter stayed off SNAP for over a year.
anchor: Cases assigned to later recertification interview dates, which leave less time to reschedule missed interviews, are over 20 percent less likely to recertify than cases assigned to interviews earlier in the month.
Cases that fail recertification due to later assignments lose an average of $600 in benefits in the following year.
one quarter remain off SNAP for over a year post-recertification
context: Tatiana Homonoff (NYU) and Jason Somerville (New York Fed), NBER Working Paper 27311 (2020), American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 13(4), 2021. Quasi-experimental: interview dates were assigned by a rule unrelated to case characteristics. Setting: San Francisco County CalFresh (SNAP) cases; the abstract gives 'over 20 percent', and the NBER version's summary elsewhere uses a different framing, so quote the abstract.

statement: Closings of Social Security Administration field offices led to a persistent 16 percent decline in the number of disability recipients in surrounding areas.
anchor: Closings lead to a persistent 16 percent decline in the number of disability recipients in surrounding areas
context: Manasi Deshpande (University of Chicago) and Yue Li (SUNY Albany), American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 11(4), 2019; peer reviewed, quasi-experimental (difference-in-differences around SSA field office closures, United States). The brief asked for the effect on applications; the abstract wording read through a fetch tool also gives a smaller fall in applications and attributes the effect mainly to crowding at neighboring offices, which should be confirmed from the paper before quoting.

statement: Pooling randomized evaluations of sector-focused training programs for low-wage workers that combine screening, occupational and soft-skills training and wraparound services, Katz, Roth, Hendra and Schaberg report substantial and persistent earnings gains of 11 to 40 percent after training, generated by moving participants into higher-wage jobs in higher-earning industries and occupations rather than just raising employment.

statement: Associated Builders and Contractors' chief economist said that if consensus forecasts hold, the construction industry will need to bring in 349,000 new workers in 2026 just to keep labor supply and demand in equilibrium, and that most of the new demand will come from retirement rather than growth in demand for construction.

statement: Associated Builders and Contractors' workforce model converts additional construction spending into worker demand at approximately 3,450 jobs per $1 billion of additional construction spending.

context: Industry group's model fitted to the historical relationship between inflation-adjusted construction spending (Census) and payroll construction employment (BLS); it is a statistical relationship, not a causal jobs multiplier for a public infrastructure program, and ignores the jobs created outside construction. A CBO or academic estimate of jobs per dollar of infrastructure spending is still needed.

statement: In the Labor Department's matched-comparison evaluation of Trade Adjustment Assistance, participants' fourth-year earnings were either $3,300 less than or about the same as those of comparison-group members, and TAA had a negative impact on total income, suggesting that additional income payments did not fully compensate for participants' lower earnings.
anchor:

comparison-group members.

TAA had a negative impact on total income, suggesting
that these additional income payments did not fully compensate for participants’ lower earnings.
context: Schochet and others, Mathematica for the Department of Labor (Obama administration), 2013. Nonexperimental: workers laid off in 2005-06 matched to UI claimants not eligible for TAA, so the low-end estimate may reflect time out of work while in training (participants spent far more time in training). Tests income support during retraining (extended Trade Readjustment Allowances) for displaced manufacturing workers, a different group from low-income parents.

statement: Using Census employer-employee data on 300,000 workers and quasi-random assignment of Trade Adjustment Assistance cases to investigators, Hyman finds TAA-approved workers have $50,000 greater cumulative earnings ten years out, though annual returns fully depreciate over that period, and that sustained returns are delivered by training rather than unemployment insurance transfers.
anchor: Using employer-employee matched Census data on 300,000 workers, I find TAA-approved workers have $50,000 greater cumulative earnings ten years out
Yet annual returns fully depreciate over the same period.
Combined with evidence that sustained returns are delivered by training rather than UI transfers
context: Benjamin Hyman (New York Fed), Census Bureau CES Working Paper 22-05 (also NBER); working paper abstract, not the peer-reviewed article. Quasi-experimental (investigator leniency design), national, about 20 years of worker data. It disagrees with the Labor Department's 2013 matched-comparison result (EV-SEC-147) because the designs differ; the training-over-transfers finding bears on whether stipends or income support alone raise later earnings.

statement: The Urban Institute's 2016 study of programs serving low-income parents reports that lack of child care can be a major barrier for low-income parents seeking education and training, and that parents may have trouble finding child care that matches their education and training schedules.
anchor: Lack of child care can be a major barrier for low-income parents seeking education and training
Parents may have trouble finding child care that matches their education and training schedules.
context: Urban Institute (nonpartisan), September 2016, qualitative interviews with 17 programs in 14 states (per Urban's summary), not an impact estimate. Wording read through a fetch tool; reviewer to confirm. The GAO upskilling report that makes a similar point (child care as a barrier to training) was not read (evidence still needed).

context: Primary law (section 7527A as added by ARPA section 9611(b)). The statute says "periodic payments in equal amounts"; Treasury paid them monthly, six payments from July to December 2021.

statement: The Census Bureau's Supplemental Poverty Measure child poverty rate fell from 9.7 percent in 2020 to 5.2 percent in 2021, the lowest on record.
anchor: The SPM child poverty rate fell 46 percent in 2021, from 9.7 percent in 2020 to 5.2 percent in 2021, a 4.5 percentage-point decline. This is the lowest SPM child poverty rate on record.
context: Official Census Bureau estimate from the CPS ASEC (published September 2022, Biden administration period). Census published a revised SPM threshold series in August 2026 (EV-SEC-207); the 2021 and 2022 child rates in this entry and EV-SEC-205 were published before that revision.

statement: The Census Bureau estimated that in 2021 the child tax credit lifted 5.3 million people out of poverty, including 2.9 million children (1 million under 6 and 1.9 million aged 6 to 17).
anchor: In 2021, the CTC lifted 5.3 million people out of poverty, including 2.9 million children (Figure below).
1 million children under 6.
1.9 million children between the ages of 6 and 17.
context: Census Bureau staff (Burns, Fox, Wilson), September 2022, Biden administration period. A static SPM accounting: it recomputes poverty without the credit and assumes no change in earnings, so it is not a causal estimate of behavioural effects. Total credit, not only the 2021 expansion (see EV-SEC-204).

statement: Census estimated that the 2021 expansion alone lifted 2.1 million children out of poverty, and that without it the 2021 SPM child poverty rate would have been 8.1 percent, 2.9 percentage points higher.
anchor: reveals that the 2021 expansions of the CTC lifted 2.1 million children out of poverty. These results can
All else equal, if the CTC had not been expanded in 2021, child poverty would have been 8.1 percent, 2.9
percentage points higher than it actually was in 2021.
context: Census Bureau working paper (Burns and Fox), 2022: holds the credit at its 2020 level, refundability and eligibility. Static, no behavioural response. The paper notes the expanded credit reached about 88 percent of children (Treasury estimate).

statement: The SPM child poverty rate more than doubled from 5.2 percent in 2021 to 12.4 percent in 2022, a 7.2 percentage-point increase.
anchor: SPM rates more than doubled for
of 18) in 2022, increasing 7.2 percentage points, from 5.2 percent
in 2021 to 12.4 percent in 2022.
context: Official Census Bureau estimate (P60-280, September 2023, Biden administration period). August 2026 threshold revision (EV-SEC-207) lowered overall SPM rates for 2019-2023 by 0.1 to 0.3 points; a child-specific revised series was not retrieved.

statement: Census attributed the rise in SPM poverty after 2021 largely to the end of pandemic stimulus payments and tax credits, and said the number of children in SPM poverty rose by over 5.0 million from 2021.
anchor: The increase was largely the result of the end of stimulus payments and tax credits in effect during the COVID-19 pandemic that had lowered the SPM rate to its lowest level ever in 2021.
the number of children in poverty using the full SPM increased by over 5.0 million children from 2021.
context: Census Bureau staff (Burns and Creamer), September 2023, Biden administration period. The expiry bundled the child credit with three rounds of stimulus payments, an expanded earned income credit and other aid, so the rise cannot be assigned to the child credit alone; inflation also peaked in 2022.

statement: On July 17, 2026, the Bureau of Labor Statistics corrected the Supplemental Poverty Measure threshold series for 2019 to 2024; Census says the corrected overall rates are 0.1 to 0.3 percentage points lower for 2019 to 2023 and 12.9% to 13.0% in 2024, with no meaningful change in the trend.
anchor: On July 17, 2026, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) corrected the SPM historical poverty threshold series from 2019 to 2024
lower than estimates published in Shrider and Bijou (2025) for 2019 to 2023 by 0.1 to 0.3 percentage points and marginally higher (12.9% to 13.0%) in 2024.
context: Census Bureau paper (Creamer, August 19, 2026), second Trump administration period; a technical correction by career staff. Flag for the dossier: SPM figures published before July 2026 (including the 5.2% and 12.4% child rates) should be re-checked against the revised series before they are quoted as final.

statement: Columbia's Center on Poverty and Social Policy estimated that the monthly child poverty rate rose from 12.1 percent in December 2021 to 17 percent in January 2022, or 3.7 million more children in poverty, after the monthly credit payments ended.
anchor: The monthly child poverty rate increased from 12.1 percent in December 2021 to 17 percent in January 2022
represents 3.7 million more children in poverty due to the expiration of the monthly Child Tax Credit payments.
context: Columbia University Center on Poverty and Social Policy (Parolin, Collyer, Curran), February 17, 2022; the authors supported the expanded credit. A monthly forecast built on the SPM, not a survey count of January 2022; Census does not publish monthly poverty.

statement: Shafer and colleagues found the first advance payment in July 2021 was associated with a roughly 26 percent drop in food insufficiency among households with children (25.9 percent in the event-study model, 16.4 percent in a difference-in-differences model).
anchor: In this cross-sectional study using repeated surveys of a nationally representative sample of US households, the introduction of advance payments for the Child Tax Credit was associated with a significant reduction in household food insufficiency of approximately 26%.
The survey had 585 170 responses, representing a weighted population size of 77 165 153 households.
a 25.9% relative reduction
a 16.4% decline
context: Peer-reviewed JAMA Network Open, January 2022 (Boston University). Quasi-experimental event study and difference-in-differences on the Census Household Pulse Survey, January 6 to August 2, 2021; households with children against households without. Self-reported food insufficiency, not an administrative measure. The authors note it covers only the first payment wave.

statement: Parolin and colleagues found the monthly credit payments reduced food insufficiency among families with children by at least 2.4 percentage points (19 percent), while the lump-sum payment instead reduced being behind on housing payments by at least 1.2 percentage points (10 percent).
anchor: among a sample of 943,568 respondents
The monthly CTC payments reduced food insufficiency among families with children by at least 2.4 percentage points (19%), but the lump-sum payment did not reduce food insufficiency.
with children were behind on housing payments by at least 1.2 percentage points (10%).
context: Columbia CPSP working paper (Parolin and others), September 2022; the authors supported the expanded credit. Difference-in-differences on the Household Pulse Survey, April 2021 to May 2022. Self-reported hardship.

statement: Pilkauskas and colleagues found the 2021 monthly child tax credit reduced the number of hardships low-income families experienced, especially food insecurity, using a parameterized difference-in-differences design.
anchor: We find that the 2021 monthly CTC reduced the number of hardships families experienced, especially food insecurity.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Population Economics, December 2024), University of Michigan and Wisconsin authors; survey-based, with very-low-income families. Shaefer is a co-founder of Rx Kids.

statement: Ananat and colleagues, using the Current Population Survey and the Census Pulse from April through December 2021, found very small, inconsistently signed and statistically insignificant effects of the expanded credit on employment and labor force participation among adults in households with children.
anchor: using data from the monthly Current Population Survey and the Census Pulse, both from April through December 2021.

we find very small, inconsistently signed, and statistically insignificant impacts of the CTC both on employment in the prior week and on active participation in the labor force among adults living in households with children.
context: NBER working paper, March 2022 (Ananat, Glasner, Hamilton, Parolin; Columbia-affiliated authors who supported the expanded credit). Observed short-window difference-in-differences: six months of payments in a pandemic year, with a temporary policy. Corinth and Meyer argue the design cannot detect a slow response (EV-SEC-221).

statement: Enriquez, Jones and Tedeschi found no strong evidence of a change in labor supply for families receiving the monthly credit, and their confidence intervals rule out a labor supply elasticity of 0.005.
anchor: We do not find strong evidence of a change in labor supply for families receiving the credit.
we rule out an extensive labor supply elasticity of 0.005
context: AEA Papers and Proceedings, 2023 (Enriquez, Jones, Tedeschi). Current Population Survey difference-in-differences and triple differences comparing families by credit size, July to December 2021. The elasticity bound refers to a temporary change in the return to work.

statement: Pilkauskas and colleagues found the monthly credit had no impact on labor supply among very-low-income families.
anchor: We find weak evidence that the credit reduced medical hardships and reliance on friends and family for food and that it had no impact on labor supply.
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Population Economics, December 2024), Michigan and Wisconsin authors. Parameterized difference-in-differences on survey data for very-low-income families. A short window in a pandemic year.

statement: Pac and Berger found a statistically nonsignificant decline in employment of approximately 344,000 to 495,000 caregivers relative to childless adults after the monthly payments began on July 15, 2021, and described the decline as at most relatively small.
anchor: monthly CTC payments were, at most, associated with a relatively small decline in employment among caregivers.
statistically nonsignificant decline in employment of approximately 344,000 to 495,000 caregivers relative to childless adults.
before and after monthly payments commenced on July 15, 2021
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, 2023), Columbia and Wisconsin authors. Event study and difference-in-differences, caregivers against childless workers. The point estimate is negative; it is not statistically distinguishable from zero. The authors report more employment among caregivers with two or more children than with one.

statement: Schanzenbach and Strain concluded that employment within broadly defined demographic groups was not reduced by the 2021 changes, but found evidence of reduced employment among mothers with relatively low levels of education.
anchor: Our review of available research suggests that employment within broadly defined demographic groups was not reduced by the 2021 CTC changes.
However, we present evidence that employment was reduced among mothers with relatively low levels of education
context: NBER working paper, June 2024 (Schanzenbach, Northwestern; Strain, AEI). A literature review plus new Current Population Survey estimates. The authors list four reasons 2021 may differ from a permanent policy: the expansion was temporary, expected to lapse, pandemic-era, and during school and child care disruption.

statement: In Schanzenbach and Strain's Current Population Survey estimates, the effect for unmarried women with some college or less was negative and statistically significant, implying a 4.5 percentage-point reduction in employment during the advance payments.
anchor: The treatment effect is negative and statistically significant and implies a 4.5 percentage-point reduction in employment during the advance CTC payments.
context: NBER working paper, June 2024 (Schanzenbach, Northwestern; Strain, AEI). A narrow subgroup (low-education, unmarried women) in a monthly CPS sample, April to December 2021; the pooled and broader-group estimates are small and not statistically significant. A subgroup estimate chosen after seeing the data is less reliable.

statement: Corinth, Meyer, Stadnicki and Wu simulated that replacing the child tax credit with a child allowance (the 2021 Build Back Better design) would lead 1.5 million workers (2.6% of working parents) to leave work, so child poverty would fall by at most 22% rather than the 34% a static count gives.
anchor: Initially ignoring any behavioral responses, we estimate that the replacement of the CTC would reduce child poverty by 34% and deep child poverty by 39%.
we estimate that this change in policy would lead 1.5 million workers (constituting 2.6% of all working parents) to exit the labor force.
child poverty would only fall by at most 22%
context: NBER working paper, October 2021 (Corinth, Meyer: AEI and University of Chicago; the authors favour work-conditioned aid). A simulation of a permanent policy using labor supply elasticities from the literature, not observed 2021 behavior. Bastian's simulation finds 367,000 (EV-SEC-219); the gap comes from elasticity assumptions and from whether higher-income and married parents respond.

statement: Bastian's preferred simulation predicted that a permanent 2021 credit would lead 367,000 parents to stop working and cut child poverty by 28 percent and deep poverty by 49 percent, or 3.1 million and 1.5 million children.
anchor: How Would a Permanent 2021 Child Tax Credit Expansion Affect Poverty and Employment?

My preferred approach predicts that 367,000 parents would stop working, and child poverty and deep poverty would decrease by 28 percent and 49 percent, representing 3.1 million and 1.5 million children, respectively.
context: National Tax Journal, May 2024 (Jacob Bastian, who served as a Biden administration CEA economist). A simulation with assumed participation elasticities (0.4 for unmarried mothers, 0.2 for other mothers, 0.05 for fathers). The paper shows child poverty still falls 20 percent under the most extreme elasticities tested.

statement: Winship (AEI) argued that applying Corinth and colleagues' elasticities to Bastian's own changes in the return to work gives about 1.8 million single mothers, or 15 percent of them, leaving work, not the 22 percent Bastian reports for the high case.
anchor: The total comes to about 1.8 million single mothers, or 15 percent of them.
Bastian, however, reports 22 percent using his unusable numbers
context: AEI commentary (Scott Winship), February 6, 2024; a conservative think tank, not peer reviewed. Winship disputes Bastian's choice of elasticities and base numbers. It argues for large work responses to the CTC and EITC, the opposite view of Bastian.

statement: Corinth and Meyer argued that the Ananat study cannot rule out substantial employment effects because of its timing assumptions, an assumption of instant response, wide confidence intervals and a lack of controls for other changes.
anchor: These flaws include incorrectly characterizing the timing and magnitude of the changes in work incentives, assuming instantaneous response when the literature suggests long lags, wide confidence intervals that include substantial effects, and a failure to control for other changing factors.
context: Note by Kevin Corinth and Bruce Meyer (University of Chicago and AEI), October 2021, authors of the competing simulation. An adversarial critique, not peer reviewed. Their point that the incentive change began when the law passed in March 2021, not in July, is a design argument, not a contrary estimate.

statement: The Niskanen Center said the Corinth simulation's estimate of 1.5 million fewer workers differs substantially from earlier estimates, which generally found limited employment effects and larger poverty reductions (usually around 40 percent).
anchor: They find that the CTC expansion proposed by the Biden administration (and currently being debated for permanent renewal by Congress) would reduce total employment by 1.5 million
which have generally found limited effects on employment as well as larger effects on poverty reduction (usually around 40 percent).
context: Niskanen Center blog post (Matt Darling), October 8, 2021; a centrist think tank that favoured an expanded credit. Opinion commentary, not peer reviewed.

statement: Strauss and colleagues estimated that aggregate employment would have been about one percentage point lower if the fully refundable 2021 credit had been in effect in 2019, and that more targeted designs could expand benefits with smaller or positive employment effects.
anchor: We estimate that aggregate employment would have declined by about one percentage point if the fully refundable 2021 version of the CTC had been in effect during 2019.
Other, more targeted, policy options could expand CTC benefits with smaller negative or positive employment effects.
context: SSRN working paper, June 2025 (Strauss, Burman, Crandall-Hollick, Hardy, McClelland; several authors at the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center). A structural simulation on Panel Study of Income Dynamics data, 1997-2019, not peer reviewed. TPC researchers generally favour a more generous credit but report a negative employment effect.

statement: Goldin and colleagues, using administrative tax records and quasi-random birth timing, found that eliminating the work requirement in a California child tax credit caused very few mothers to exit the labor force, with a 95% confidence interval that excludes reductions over one-third of one percent.
anchor: Eliminating the work requirement caused very few mothers to exit the labor force; our 95% confidence interval excludes reductions over one-third of one percent.
context: NBER working paper, April 2024 (Goldin, Homonoff, Lal, Lurie, Michelmore, Unrath). Quasi-experimental, administrative tax data, California only (the state YCTC, a smaller credit than the 2021 federal one). This is the most precise estimate of the pure work-requirement effect found; it is not a federal estimate. The brief's "Lourie et al. 2025" was not found; this paper (with author Lurie) is the closest match.

statement: The National Academies report estimated that child poverty costs the nation roughly $800 billion to $1.1 trillion a year in lost adult productivity, higher crime costs and higher health costs.
anchor: Studies estimate that child poverty costs the nation roughly between $800 billion and $1.1 trillion annually in terms of lost adult productivity, the increased costs of crime, and increased health expenditures.
context: National Academies consensus study report, 2019, requested by Congress (Trump first administration period). A synthesis of prior economic studies, not a new estimate; the range is wide and depends on the causal effect assumed for income on adult outcomes.

statement: The National Academies modelled two packages that would cut child poverty in half at $90.7 billion and $108.8 billion a year; the second included a $225 a month child allowance.
anchor: This package of programs would reduce both poverty and deep poverty by half, at an estimated cost of $90.7 billion per year.
Instituting a new child allowance that pays a monthly benefit of $225 per month ($2,700 per year) to families of all children under age 17.
This package is estimated to cost $108.8 billion per year
context: National Academies consensus report, 2019 (this entry omits the lower-cost $44.5 billion package, which cut child poverty by 36 percent). Simulation of packages on pre-2018 tax law with labor supply elasticities; the means-tested package added about 400,000 workers and the universal package over 600,000 jobs on the committee's elasticities. Dollar costs are 2015-law-era and not current.

statement: In the Baby's First Years randomized trial, after four years the $333 a month transfer, against $20 a month, had no statistically significant effect on four preregistered child outcomes: language, executive function, social-emotional problems and high-frequency brain activity.
anchor: randomized to receive either $333/month or $20/month for the first several years of their children's lives.
we find no statistically significant impacts of the cash transfers on four preregistered primary outcomes (language, executive function, social-emotional problems, and high-frequency brain activity)
context: NBER working paper, May 2025 (Noble, Magnuson, Duncan, Gennetian, Yoshikawa and others). RCT of 1,000 mothers below the poverty line recruited in 2018-19 in New York, New Orleans, Omaha and Minneapolis-St. Paul; foundation-funded; four years of payments during the pandemic when other aid was large. The lead authors said the result surprised them. Possible explanations include effects emerging later.

statement: In the first Baby's First Years result, infants in the high-cash group showed more power in high-frequency EEG bands at about age one (n = 435), although the significance of estimates varied with the analytic specification.
anchor: using resting electroencephalography (EEG; n = 435).
Indeed, infants in the high-cash gift group showed more power in high-frequency bands.
although the significance of estimates varied with the analytic specification.
context: PNAS, January 2022 (Troller-Renfree, Costanzo, Duncan, Magnuson, Gennetian and others). RCT subsample; the pandemic truncated in-person data collection. The authors cautioned against policy conclusions from the first year; the age-four direct assessments did not confirm a lasting effect (EV-SEC-227).

statement: AEI argued that income assistance requiring work, in the form of the EITC, has shown the strongest evidence of boosting kids' development, while evidence for support not tied to work is weaker or relies on the food stamp rollout over half a century ago.
anchor: Income assistance that requires work, in the form of the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), has shown the strongest evidence of boosting kids’ development.
The evidence for support not tied to work is generally weaker or relies on evidence from over half a century ago
locator: Body, third paragraph after the block quote
context: AEI commentary (Sarah Jeddy), July 30, 2025; a conservative think tank, not peer reviewed. It also notes the trial ran during the pandemic and results could differ in normal times.

statement: In the OpenResearch randomized trial (two states, $1,000 a month for three years versus $50 a month), treated participants' income excluding the transfers fell by about $1,900 a year, labor market participation fell 4.2 percentage points, and work hours fell by 1-2 hours a week, with partners reducing hours by a comparable amount.
anchor: randomized into receiving $1,000 per month unconditionally for three years, with a control group of 2,000 participants receiving $50/month.
excluding the transfers to fall by about $1,900/year relative to the control group and a 4.2 percentage point decrease in labor market participation.
Participants reduced their work hours as a result of the transfers by 1–2 hours/week and participants’ partners reduced their work hours by a comparable amount.
context: Quarterly Journal of Economics 141(4), published August 2026 (Vivalt, Rhodes, Bartik, Broockman, Krause, Miller). RCT of 3,000 low-income adults aged 21-40 in Illinois and Texas, 2020-2023; funded by Sam Altman via OpenResearch. Not parents specifically and unconditional at far higher amounts than the child credit. The July 2024 working paper reported different figures (about $1,500 a year, a 2.0 point drop, 1.3 to 1.4 hours a week); this entry uses the published version.

statement: A difference-in-differences study found Rx Kids, which pays every expectant mother in Flint cash in pregnancy and infancy, was associated with a preterm birth rate 2.7 percentage points lower and a low birthweight share 4.2 percentage points lower than in matched cities, from baselines of 15.1% and 15.8%.
anchor: 15.1% (445 of 2940) of births in Flint were preterm and 15.8% (465 of 2943) were low birthweight
Rx Kids was associated with a decrease in the preterm birth rate by 2.7 percentage points
in the proportion of infants born with low birthweight by 4.2 percentage points
locator: Summary, Findings (the journal prints decimal points as raised dots)
context: The Lancet Public Health, 2026 (the programme pays US$1,500 mid-pregnancy and $500 a month to age 1; the paper also reports relative reductions of 13-18% and 22-27%, not re-checked; funded by the Mott and Jacob family foundations; Agarwal, Shaefer, Zamani-Hank, Finegood, LaChance). Quasi-experimental, one city (Flint, Michigan, a low-income community) with a universal programme starting January 2024; the authors include the programme's co-founder. An undergraduate thesis found little robust evidence on core birth outcomes with synthetic control methods (not peer reviewed), so the estimate depends on the comparison group. Anchors re-checked against the published summary by the dossier author, 2026-11-12.

statement: Hoynes, Schanzenbach and Almond found that access to food stamps in childhood, as the program rolled out across counties from 1961 to 1975, led to a significant reduction in metabolic syndrome in adulthood and, for women, an increase in economic self-sufficiency.
anchor: We focus on the introduction of the Food Stamp Program, which was rolled out across counties between 1961 and 1975.
access to food stamps in childhood leads to a significant reduction in the incidence of metabolic syndrome and, for women, an increase in economic self-sufficiency.
context: American Economic Review, April 2016. Quasi-experimental (county rollout dates), Panel Study of Income Dynamics. In-kind food aid, not cash; mid-twentieth-century levels of deprivation were far higher than today, which limits transfer to a modern child benefit.

statement: Aizer and colleagues found that male children of accepted Mothers' Pension applicants lived one year longer than those of rejected mothers, with one-third more schooling and higher adult income; the transfers generally represented 12-25 percent of family income.
anchor: Male children of accepted applicants lived one year longer than those of rejected mothers.
They also obtained one-third more years of schooling, were less likely to be underweight, and had higher income in adulthood than children of rejected mothers.
The transfers generally represented 12–25 percent of family income
context: American Economic Review, April 2016. Natural-experiment design comparing accepted and rejected applicants (Mothers' Pension, 1911-1935, 11 states, children born 1900-1925). The authors caution about drawing conclusions for the twenty-first century.

statement: Canada's Canada Child Benefit pays up to $8,157 a year for each child under 6 and $6,883 for each child aged 6 to 17 for the benefit year starting July 2026; the amounts start to be reduced when adjusted family net income exceeds $38,237, at 7% for one child, 13.5% for two, 19% for three and 23% for four or more up to $82,847.

context: Official Government of Canada programme parameters for the benefit year July 2026 to June 2027 (Carney Liberal government). No phase-in: the benefit is paid at the maximum from the first dollar of income, so there is no work requirement or earnings test.

statement: Above $82,847 of adjusted family net income, the Canada Child Benefit reduction is a fixed amount plus a lower rate: $3,123 plus 3.2% for one child, $6,022 plus 5.7% for two, $8,476 plus 8% for three, and $10,260 plus 9.5% for four or more.

locator: "How you can expect to receive" section of the guide
context: Official Government of Canada parameters, July 2026 to June 2027. The two-step reduction means high marginal tax rates only in the middle range ($38,237 to $82,847), where rates reach 23% for large families, adding to income tax.

statement: The Canada Child Benefit is a tax-free monthly benefit adjusted for inflation, paid from July to June on the previous calendar year's adjusted family net income; about 3.5 million families received $26.3 billion in 2023-24.
anchor: The Canada Child Benefit (CCB) is a tax-free, monthly benefit adjusted for inflation

The CCB is paid monthly to eligible parents over a 12-month period from July to June each benefit year, with the CCB entitlement based on the adjusted family net income (AFNI) for the calendar year before the beginning of the benefit year.
About 3.5 million families received the CCB in 2023-24, Footnote 4 receiving $26.3 billion in total benefits.
context: Department of Finance Canada tax expenditure report, 2026. Official description of an income-tested monthly benefit assessed by the Canada Revenue Agency on the annual tax return; the benefit has been indexed to inflation since 2018.

statement: The Canada Revenue Agency determines each year whether a family is entitled to child benefit payments when the family files its tax return.
anchor: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) determines if you are entitled to CCB payments each year when you file your tax return.
context: Official Canada Revenue Agency description. Delivery through tax filing means non-filers do not receive the benefit automatically, a coverage gap noted in Canadian research.

statement: Under Canada's Market Basket Measure (2018 base), the poverty rate for people under 18 was 9.4% in 2019, 4.7% in 2020, 6.4% in 2021, 9.9% in 2022 and 10.7% in 2023.
anchor: Persons living below the poverty line (Market Basket Measure, 2018 base), Canada
locator: Table 3, rows "Persons under 18 years" (share of population)
context: Statistics Canada Canadian Income Survey (Table 11-10-0135-01), May 2025. The 2020-21 dip reflects pandemic benefits that were withdrawn by 2022; the later rise happened with the CCB unchanged in structure. The 2018-base line was replaced by the 2023-base line in November 2025.

statement: Under the 2023-base Market Basket Measure, the poverty rate for people under 18 was 5.2% in 2020, 7.0% in 2021, 10.7% in 2022, 12.1% in 2023 and 11.5% in 2024.
locator: Table 3, rows "Persons under 18 years" (share of population)
context: Statistics Canada Canadian Income Survey, April 29, 2026, Table 11-10-0135-01. The 2023-base series became official in November 2025 and starts in 2020; rates are higher than the 2018-base series for the same years, so the two series must not be spliced.

statement: The Government of Canada reported that the child poverty rate was 10.7 percent in 2023, down from 16.3 percent in 2015.
anchor: the poverty rate for children was 10.7 percent in 2023 and is higher than the overall poverty rate of 10.2 percent, but continues to reflect a significant decrease from the poverty rate of 16.3 percent in 2015.
context: Employment and Social Development Canada briefing note, June 2025 (Carney government), citing the 2018-base Market Basket Measure. A ministerial briefing note is promotional about its own programme and attributes the fall to the CCB; the fall also coincides with pandemic aid, rising wages and a tight labor market.

statement: Baker, Messacar and Stabile found that both the 2015 expansion of the Universal Child Care Benefit and the 2016 Canada Child Benefit reduced child poverty, with the CCB having the greater effect, and found no labor supply response on the extensive or intensive margin.
anchor: within the context of the 2015 expansion of the Canadian Universal Child Care Benefit (UCCB) and the 2016 introduction of the Canada Child Benefit (CCB).

Our analysis indicates that both reforms reduced child poverty, although the Canada Child Benefit had the greater effect. We find no evidence of a labor supply response to either of the program reforms on either the extensive or intensive margins.
context: NBER working paper, March 2021 (Baker, Messacar, Stabile; published by University of Chicago Press, 2023). Difference-in-differences comparing single mothers with single childless women, tax-filer data (LAD), Canadian Income Survey and Labour Force Survey. Canada is a different institutional setting: income-tested, universal child care later, and no phase-in work requirement.

statement: The same paper warned that its two data sources disagreed on the size of the CCB effect: using the Market Basket Measure and the Canadian Income Survey, the reduction following the CCB was much smaller, partly because poverty also fell for the childless comparison group.
anchor: the reduction following the introduction of the CCB is much smaller.
it is much smaller following the introduction of the CCB, primarily because poverty declined for both treatment and control groups.
the difference in the inference from the LAD and CIS prevents strong conclusions about the relative impacts of the two policy reforms.
context: Baker, Messacar and Stabile (NBER w28556, 2021). The authors note that the childless-women control group is imperfect and that non-experimental evaluation has limits; the single-mother low-income-measure fall of about 5 points (a 12% decline) is in the administrative data only.

statement: The Universal Credit (Removal of Two Child Limit) Act received Royal Assent on 18 March 2026, and removal of the two-child limit from Universal Credit takes effect from 6 April 2026.
anchor: The Universal Credit (Removal of Two Child Limit Act) received Royal Assent on 18 March 2026.
The removal of the two-child limit from Universal Credit takes effect from 6 April 2026.
context: UK Department for Work and Pensions press release, 19 March 2026 (Labour government). Statutory fact reported by the government; the estimates in its text are promotional.

statement: The UK government estimates removing the two-child limit would leave 450,000 fewer children in relative low income after housing costs in the final year of the parliament (financial year ending 2030), compared with baseline projections.
anchor: It is estimated that there will be 450,000 fewer children in relative low income after housing costs in the final year of parliament (financial year ending (FYE) 2030) as a result of removing the two-child limit, compared to baseline projections.
context: UK Department for Work and Pensions microsimulation (Policy Simulation Model on the Family Resources Survey, consistent with OBR November 2025 forecasts), published with the Budget of 26 November 2025. Government analysis of its own policy; static aside from a take-up response. The Commons Library gives the cost as £2.4 billion in 2026/27 rising to £3.2 billion in 2030/31 (EV-SEC-245).

statement: The House of Commons Library summary of the November 2025 Budget says removing the two-child limit is expected to cut the number of children in poverty by 450,000 by 2029/30, at a forecast cost of £2.4 billion in 2026/27 rising to £3.2 billion in 2030/31.
anchor: This change is expected to reduce the number of children in poverty by 450,000 by 2029/30, compared with what it otherwise would have been. The cost is forecast to be £2.4 billion in 2026/27 and then rise, reaching £3.2 billion in 2030/31.
context: House of Commons Library, a nonpartisan research service, November 27, 2025, relaying the Office for Budget Responsibility's costing.

statement: The Institute for Fiscal Studies estimated that reversing the two-child limit would lift 540,000 children over the absolute poverty line at an eventual cost of £2.5 billion a year, but that 70,000 of the poorest households would see the gains partly or fully wiped out by the household benefit cap.
anchor: Reversing the two-child limit would pull 540,000 children over the absolute poverty line
This would be at an eventual cost of £2.5 billion a year
But 70,000 of the poorest households subject to the two-child limit would see the gains from its reversal partially or fully wiped out by the household benefit cap
context: Institute for Fiscal Studies (independent UK research institute), Green Budget, October 2024, funded by the Nuffield Foundation and produced with Citi. Uses the absolute poverty line (the government uses relative low income), so numbers differ from the DWP figure.

statement: Eissa and Liebman found that between 1984-1986 and 1988-1990 single women with children increased their relative labor force participation by up to 2.8 percentage points after the 1986 expansion, with no change in relative hours for those already working.
anchor: We find that between 1984–1986 and 1988–1990, single women with children increased their relative labor force participation by up to 2.8 percentage points. We observe no change in the relative hours worked by single women with children who were already in the labor force.
context: Quarterly Journal of Economics, May 1996. Difference-in-differences around the Tax Reform Act of 1986, single mothers versus single women without children, Current Population Survey. A small expansion; Kleven (2024) questions whether such designs isolate the credit.

statement: Meyer and Rosenbaum found that a large share of the 1984-1996 increase in work by single mothers can be attributed to the EITC and other tax changes, with smaller shares for welfare benefit cuts, waivers, training and child care programs.
anchor: During 1984–1996, welfare and tax policy were changed to encourage work by single mothers.

We show that a large share of the increase in work by single mothers can be attributed to the EITC and other tax changes, with smaller shares for welfare benefit cuts, welfare waivers, training programs and child care programs.
context: Quarterly Journal of Economics, August 2001 (Meyer, a co-author of the Corinth et al. simulation). Combines several policy changes; the 1990s welfare reform overlap is the confounder Kleven emphasises.

statement: Hoynes and Patel found that a policy-induced $1000 increase in the EITC reduced by 8.4 percentage points the share of single-mother families with after-tax-and-transfer income below 100% of poverty, and that static counts may understate the EITC's antipoverty effect by almost 50 percent by ignoring its effect on earnings.
anchor: a policy-induced $1000 increase in the EITC leads to an 8.4 percentage point reduction in the share of families with after tax and transfer income below 100% poverty.
static calculations of the anti-poverty effects of the EITC (such as those released based on the Supplemental Poverty Measure) may be underestimated by almost 50 percent.
context: Journal of Human Resources 53(4), 2018. Quasi-experimental, single mothers with children versus those without or with fewer children, 1986 and 1993 expansions; the employment-driven part of the result rests on the contested extensive-margin effect (Kleven 2024).

statement: Hoynes, Miller and Simon found that a $1,000 treatment-on-the-treated increase in EITC income leads to a 2 to 3 percent decline in low birth weight.
anchor: a $1,000 treatment-on-the-treated leads to a 2 to 3 percent decline in low birth weight.
context: American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, February 2015. Difference-in-differences across federal EITC expansions, single low-education mothers. Evidence of mechanism: more prenatal care, less smoking.

statement: Bastian and Michelmore found that an additional $1,000 of EITC exposure when a child is 13-18 raises the likelihood of completing high school by 1.3%, college by 4.2% and young-adult employment by 1.0%, and earnings by 2.2%, mainly through higher family earnings.
anchor: an additional $1,000 in EITC exposure when a child is 13–18 years old increases the likelihood of completing high school (1.3%), completing college (4.2%), and being employed as a young adult (1.0%) and earnings by 2.2%.
the primary channel through which the EITC improves these outcomes is increases in pretax family earnings.
context: Journal of Labor Economics 36(4), 2018. Quasi-experimental use of four decades of federal and state EITC variation. Relies on the credit raising family earnings, which Kleven (2024) contests for the extensive margin.

statement: Kleven found that apart from the federal 1993 reform, EITC expansions are not associated with clear and robust effects on employment, with about 500 event-study estimates distributed symmetrically around zero, and argued the 1993 gains align more with welfare reform and the economy than with the EITC.
anchor: Apart from the federal 1993 reform, EITC expansions are not associated with any clear and robust effects on employment. Treatment impact estimates from about 500 event studies are symmetrically distributed around zero.
the paper shows that these increases align more closely with confounding effects from welfare reform and the macroeconomy than with the EITC.
context: NBER working paper 2019; published in the Journal of Public Economics 236 (August 2024), not Econometrica as the brief had it (Henrik Kleven, Princeton). Re-analysis of every state and federal EITC reform since 1975 using event studies. The estimate concerns employment entry, not income, poverty or child outcomes; the credit may still raise incomes of workers.

statement: Schanzenbach and Strain, studying all federal expansions since 1975, found that a $1,000 increase in the maximum credit is associated with a 3.0 to 3.3 percentage-point increase in employment among unmarried mothers with low education, and reconciled their results with Kleven by adopting his methodological choices.
anchor: This paper takes a longer view, studying all federal expansions since the program’s inception in 1975. We find robust evidence that EITC expansions increase the extensive margin of labor supply.
a $1,000 increase in the size of the maximum credit is associated with a 3.0 to 3.3 percentage point increase in employment among unmarried mothers with low levels of education.
We are able to reconcile our results by adopting his methodological choices.
context: NBER working paper 2020, published in Tax Policy and the Economy 35 (2021) (Schanzenbach, Northwestern; Strain, AEI). Directly answers Kleven's working paper: they say the differences come from business-cycle controls, sample choice (all unmarried women) and the outcome measure (worked last week versus last year).

statement: The Paycheck Plus randomized trial in New York City (about 6,000 single adults without dependent children) found the larger credit raised employment by 2.6 percentage points in Year 2 and 2.1 in Year 3 (1.9 over three years) and after-bonus earnings by $635 a year.
anchor: where over 6,000 low-income single adults without dependent children enrolled in the study in late 2013.
increased employment rates in Year 2 and Year 3, by 2.6 percentage points and 2.1 percentage points, respectively.
Over the full three-year period, the program increased the average annual employment rate by 1.9 percentage points.
for a statistically significant increase of $635, or about a 6 percent increase
context: MDRC (nonprofit evaluator), 2018. RCT in New York City, bonus up to $2,000 for childless adults earning up to $30,000, 2014-2016. Effects larger for women and disadvantaged men. The sample is a self-selected urban group.

statement: The Paycheck Plus randomized trial in Atlanta (about 4,000 single adults without dependent children) increased after-bonus earnings by $775 in the first year but neither increased nor reduced employment over three years.
anchor: about 4,000 single adults with low incomes were recruited to take part in the study.
for a statistically significant increase of $775, or about 8 percent.
It neither increased nor reduced employment during the program’s three years.
context: MDRC (nonprofit evaluator), 2022. RCT in Atlanta, 2017-2019; unlike New York, the offer did not raise employment, and it did not reduce work effort in the phase-out range, the design concern. Low bonus receipt (45 percent of eligibles in Year 3) limits the dose.

statement: For 2021 only, ARPA doubled the childless EITC phase-in and phase-out rates from 7.65% to 15.3%, raised the maximum credit from $543 to $1,502, and lowered the minimum age from 25 to 19 for most workers; CRS put the one-year cost at $11.9 billion.

context: CRS (nonpartisan) description of ARPA section 9621, 2021. Temporary; expired after tax year 2021. The credit reverted to a maximum of $543 (indexed) and ages 25 to 64.

statement: The Tax Policy Center reported that 4.3 million young workers without children received an average credit of almost $900 in 2021 from the temporary childless EITC expansion.

context: Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center (nonpartisan), 2024, using IRS-based tabulations. A count of recipients and credit size, not a labor supply effect. The Paycheck Plus RCTs are the experimental evidence on childless credits (EV-SEC-254, EV-SEC-255).

Improper payments include overclaims from errors as well as fraud; the rate is an estimate from audits and has been above 20 percent for years.

statement: Section 70104 of the 2025 reconciliation law made the earlier law's child tax credit changes permanent and permanently raised the maximum credit to $2,200 per child (adjusted for inflation), with a Social Security number required for the taxpayer and the child.
anchor: Section 70104 of the law
This provision makes permanent the TJCA's changes to the credit and permanently raises the maximum credit to $2,200 per child (adjusted for inflation).

This provision also requires the taxpayer to provide a work-eligible SSN for themselves (or, if married filing jointly, either themselves or their spouse) and the child for whom they are claiming the credit.
context: CRS (nonpartisan) description of the enacted law (P.L. 119-21, July 4, 2025). The refundable portion is still limited to $1,700 per child for 2025 and requires earned income; CRS notes the credit applies from 2025 onward.

reducing the child poverty rate from 13.3% to 8.8% (or by 33.6%) and moving an additional 3.3 million children above the poverty line.

Overall, 7 percent of employees report unmet need for leave for a qualifying FMLA reason in the past 12
months, an increase from 5 percent in 2012. Reporting unmet need for leave for a qualifying FMLA
reason is more common among “low-wage workers” (9 percent), defined as those making less than $15
per hour, than among other workers (6 percent).
context: DOL/Abt 2018 Employee Survey, self-reported over the prior 12 months.

statement: Among employees with unmet need for leave in 2018, the most common reason for not taking it was inability to afford unpaid leave (66 percent), followed by fear of losing their job (45 percent).
anchor:
The most common reason employees give for not taking needed leave is inability to afford
unpaid leave (66 percent). The next most common is fear of losing their job (45 percent).
context: DOL/Abt 2018 Employee Survey. The unmet-need group in this finding includes leave to care for a non-immediate family member as well as FMLA-qualifying reasons; respondents could give several reasons. Small sample of employees with unmet need.

statement: After taking leave, 87 percent of employees returned to the same employer and position, but 18 percent of low-wage workers reported losing a job as a result of taking leave, against 5 percent of other workers.

leave.
context: DOL/Abt 2018 Employee Survey, self-reported job loss; no check against employer records.

statement: As of September 2026, 13 states (including DC) operate mandatory paid family and medical leave insurance programs offering 12 to 52 weeks of total benefits, with family leave limited to 8 to 12 weeks; Maryland and Virginia have enacted programs that are not scheduled to pay benefits until 2028.
anchor:
As of September 2026, 13 states (including DC)
operate such programs, which offer 12 to 52 weeks of total benefits to eligible workers in a benefit year (in those states,
family leave insurance benefits that may be used, for example, to care for a new child or for a family member with a serious
health condition are generally limited to 8 to 12 weeks).

Maryland and Virginia have enacted laws establishing mandatory family and medical
leave insurance programs but are not scheduled to start paying benefits until 2028.
locator: CRS R44835, Summary and State-Run section
context: CRS (nonpartisan), September 2026. The programs are mandatory (employers and employees cannot generally opt out). New Hampshire and Vermont have voluntary plans. Brief expected Maryland in 2028, which matches CRS; Virginia (enacted 2026) is also 2028.

statement: California paid family leave benefits became payable on July 1, 2004, New Jersey on July 1, 2009, Rhode Island on January 1, 2014 and New York on January 1, 2018; California, New Jersey, New York and Rhode Island built on existing temporary disability insurance programs.
