context: CRS footnote 27 (nonpartisan). Start dates for Washington (2020), DC (2020), Massachusetts (2021), Connecticut (2022), Oregon (2023) and Colorado (2024) are not in the saved text and are still needed from the state pages.

statement: State weekly benefits range from 50% to 100% of average weekly earnings up to a cap; in 2026 the caps range from $170 per week for New York medical leave to $1,765 per week for California; most states use a progressive formula.
anchor:
Weekly leave insurance benefit amounts range from 50% to 100% of an employee’s average
weekly earnings, up to a maximum amount. Most states use or plan to use a progressive benefit
formula (i.e., lower earning workers receive a higher share of their average weekly wages).29 All
states cap benefits at a maximum weekly amount, which in 2026 range from $170 per week for
MLI benefits in New York to $1,765 per week for FLI or MLI benefits in California.
context: CRS (nonpartisan), September 2026.

statement: All state programs are financed by payroll contributions: employees alone pay in California, Connecticut and Rhode Island; employees pay for family leave and employees and employers share medical leave in Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York and Washington; employers and employees share the whole cost in Colorado, Delaware, Maine, Maryland, Minnesota, Oregon and Virginia; DC is employer financed.
anchor:
All mandatory state leave insurance programs are financed through payroll contributions, with
some variation in how contributions are allocated between employers and employees. Program
benefits in California, Connecticut, and Rhode Island are financed by employee payroll
contributions. In Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, and Washington, employees finance FLI
benefits, and employees and employers jointly finance MLI benefits. Employers and employees
jointly finance total program benefits (both FLI and MLI) in Colorado, Delaware, Maine,
Maryland, Minnesota, Oregon, and Virginia. DC program benefits are financed by employers.
context: CRS (nonpartisan), September 2026. This is the state design; the 2025 FAMILY Act bill text has no payroll tax provision (see the FAMILY Act financing entry).

Tax credits cannot be claimed for leave paid by state or
local governments, or for leave that is required by state or
local law. Thus, this tax incentive does not reduce the cost
of providing leave in jurisdictions where employers are
required to do so by a state or local authority. However, the

A tax credit can only be claimed for wages paid for family
and medical leave. General paid leave (e.g., vacation,
personal, or sick leave) that is not specifically set aside for
an FMLA-qualifying purpose is not considered PFML leave
for purposes of the tax credit. Family and medical leave is
restricted to leave associated with (1) the birth of a child or
placement of an adopted or foster child with the employee;
(2) a serious health condition of the employee or the
employee’s spouse, child, or parent; (3) an exigency arising
out of the fact that a close relative is a member of the
Armed Forces and on covered active duty; or (4) to care for
a seriously ill or injured covered servicemember who is a
close relative of the employee. Per IRS guidance for the tax
credit, an employer’s PFML policy may allow leave to be
used to care for a broader group of individuals than allowed
under FMLA (such as adding grandparents) and still be a
valid PFML policy for purposes of the tax credit. However,
the credit may only be claimed for caregiving that qualifies
for FMLA-protected leave, which is generally limited to
caregiving for a child, spouse, or parent.
To claim the credit, an employer generally must have a
written family and medical leave policy in effect. The
policy cannot exclude certain classifications of employees.
For employers, the amount of wages and salaries deducted
as a business expense is reduced by the amount of credit
claimed. Further, the credit cannot be claimed for wages
that have been used for another tax credit (to avoid a double
tax benefit). The credit is part of the general business credit,
meaning that it is subject to limitations (generally, it can be
used to offset up to 75% of tax liability). Unused credits
from the current tax year can be carried back one year
(offsetting the prior year’s tax liability) or carried forward
up to 20 years to offset future tax liability. The credit is
allowed against the alternative minimum tax (AMT).

Legislative History
The employer credit for paid family and medical leave was
enacted as part of P.L. 115-97. When enacted, this credit
was made available for two years, 2018 and 2019. The
credit was extended through 2020 in the Further
Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2020 (P.L. 116-94) and
through 2025 in the Taxpayer Certainty and Disaster Tax
Relief Act of 2020 (Division EE of P.L. 116-260). The
credit was made permanent by P.L. 119-21.

statement: Using March CPS data from 1999-2010, Rossin-Slater, Ruhm and Waldfogel found California's program doubled use of maternity leave from an average of around 3 to 6 weeks and increased the usual weekly work hours of employed mothers of one-to-three-year-olds by 10 to 17%.

context: Peer reviewed (JPAM 2013); difference-in-differences with comparison groups of older-child mothers, childless women and other states; tried in California, 2004 program (six weeks at 55%). The authors call the labor market evidence "more equivocal." Co-authored by Ruhm, who also wrote the Baum study.

statement: Baum and Ruhm found, using a national youth survey cohort, that California's program raised leave use by almost five weeks for the average covered mother and two to three days for the father, and was associated with higher work and employment probabilities for mothers nine to 12 months after birth.

statement: Using IRS and SSA tax data and a regression discontinuity in time, Bailey, Byker, Patel and Ramnath found no evidence that California's 2004 Paid Family Leave Act increased women's employment, earnings or childbearing, and found it reduced employment and earnings of first-time mothers roughly a decade after birth.

The brief recalled larger 2019-version figures (about 7% fewer employed, 8% lower earnings); the revised abstract quotes no percentages, and a paragraph of the paper says no negative effects for mothers who already had children. Short-run effects were not negative. Identifies effects of the sharp rise in weeks at the 2004 launch, six weeks at 55%.

statement: The 2025 law's new $6,000 deduction for people age 65 or older runs from 2025 through 2028 and is reduced by 6% of modified adjusted gross income above $75,000 ($150,000 for joint filers).
anchor: It also temporarily creates a new $6,000 deduction for taxpayers (and their spouses, if married filing jointly) who are age 65 or older, from 2025 through 2028. This amount is reduced by 6% of a taxpayer's modified adjusted gross income above $75,000 ($150,000 for those married filing jointly).
context: CRS (nonpartisan) description of section 70103 of P.L. 119-21. The deduction ends after tax year 2028, so it is not in force in 2029 unless extended. It adds a 6 percent phase-out layer for older filers in its range.

statement: SNAP's gross income standard is 130 percent of the federal poverty level for households without an elderly or disabled member, who must meet both the gross and the net income standards; categorically eligible households need meet neither.
anchor: Households which do not contain an elderly or disabled member shall meet both the net income eligibility standards and the gross income eligibility standards for SNAP. Households which are categorically eligible as defined in § 273.2(j)(2) or 273.2(j)(4) do not have to meet either the gross or net income eligibility standards.

(i) The income eligibility standards for the 48 contiguous States and the District of Columbia, Guam and the Virgin Islands shall be 130 percent of the Federal income poverty levels for the 48 contiguous States and the District of Columbia.
context: USDA regulation (eCFR, November 2026). The net-income standard is 100 percent of poverty by statute (7 U.S.C. 2014(c)); the 30 percent benefit reduction and the 20 percent earnings deduction are EV-HOU-417 and EV-HOU-418.

anchor: The first $20 of any unearned income in a month other than income in the form of in-kind support and maintenance received in the household of another (see § 416.1131) and income based on need.
context: 20 CFR 416.1124(c)(12). Dollar-for-dollar reduction above the exclusion is stated in SSA's payment page (EV-SEC-524).

statement: The maximum federal SSI payment for 2027 is $1,029 a month for an eligible individual and $1,544 for an eligible individual with an eligible spouse, and the monthly amount is reduced by subtracting monthly countable income.
anchor: SSI amounts for 2027 The monthly maximum Federal amounts for 2027 are $1,029 for an eligible individual, $1,544 for an eligible individual with an eligible spouse, and $516 for an essential person.
The monthly amount is reduced by subtracting monthly countable income.
context: SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, second Trump administration; the 2027 amount follows a 3.6 percent cost-of-living adjustment announced in October 2026. The 2026 individual amount is the page's unrounded $11,929.46 a year, or $994 a month (arithmetic; not quoted). SSI is federal; many states add a supplement.

statement: Substantial gainful activity is $1,690 a month for non-blind and $2,830 for blind beneficiaries in 2026, rising to $1,770 and $2,950 in 2027; a person earning more than the amount is ordinarily considered to be engaging in it.
anchor: A person who is earning more than a certain monthly amount (net of impairment-related work expenses) is ordinarily considered to be engaging in SGA.
context: SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, second Trump administration. The SGA amount is the SSDI earnings cliff: beneficiaries earning above it (after a trial work period) lose cash benefits (EV-SEC-545).

statement: LIHEAP state programs may serve households with incomes up to the greater of 150 percent of the state's poverty level or 60 percent of state median income.
context: 2024 edition of the Code. LIHEAP is a block grant, so each state sets its own line within this ceiling, and many give flat grants rather than a phase-out. LIHEAP receipt also fed SNAP's utility allowance until the 2025 law limited that (EV-SEC-508).

statement: Federal law sets school lunch income guidelines at 130 percent of the poverty guideline for free lunches and 185 percent for reduced-price lunches.
anchor: The income guidelines for determining eligibility for free lunches shall be 130 percent of the applicable family size income levels
The income guidelines for determining eligibility for reduced price lunches for any school year shall be 185 percent of the applicable family size income levels
context: 2024 edition of the Code. Households on SNAP or TANF are directly certified without a separate income test, which is a coordination example. School meals are a cliff (free to reduced to full price), not a phase-out.

statement: WIC state agencies may set income guidelines equal to the reduced-price school meal guidelines or identical to state or local free or reduced-price health care guidelines.
anchor: The State agency may prescribe income guidelines either equaling the income guidelines established under section 9 of the National School Lunch Act for reduced-price school meals or identical to State or local guidelines for free or reduced-price health care.
context: 7 CFR 246.7(d)(1). The reduced-price school meal line is 185 percent of poverty (EV-SEC-527), so WIC's usual line is 185 percent. WIC participants are adjunctively income-eligible through SNAP, TANF or Medicaid.

statement: Each state's Child Care and Development Block Grant plan must provide continued assistance after a family's income exceeds the state's initial limit, if family income does not exceed 85 percent of state median income, and must keep a child eligible for not less than 12 months before redetermination.
anchor: The plan shall describe the policies and procedures that are in place to allow for provision of continued assistance to carry out this subchapter, at the beginning of a new eligibility period under clause (i)(I), for children of parents who are working or attending a job training or educational program and whose family income exceeds the State's income limit to initially qualify for such assistance, if the family income for the family involved does not exceed 85 percent of the State median income for a family of the same size.
for not less than 12 months before the State or designated local entity redetermines the eligibility of the child
context: The 2014 reauthorization of the CCDBG (Obama administration; bipartisan). The "graduated phaseout" requirement is a continued-assistance rule; it does not require any particular copayment slope. HHS's May 2026 final rule rescinded the 7 percent copayment cap (EV-CAR-510).

statement: CCDF eligibility requires a child to live with a family whose income does not exceed 85 percent of state median income, based on the most recent Census Bureau data, for a family of the same size.
anchor: (2)(i) Reside with a family whose income does not exceed 85 percent of the State's median income (SMI), which must be based on the most recent SMI data that is published by the Bureau of the Census, for a family of the same size; and
context: 45 CFR 98.20(a)(2)(i) (eCFR, November 2026). The 85 percent is a federal ceiling; states set lower entry lines and most serve only a fraction of eligible families (EV-SEC-563 for Colorado).

statement: There are no federal rules on the amount of TANF cash benefits; states alone determine them, and a family with other income often receives a reduced benefit.
anchor: There are no federal rules that help determine the amount of TANF cash benefits paid to a family.
Benefit amounts are determined solely by the states.
Families with income other than TANF often are paid a reduced benefit.
context: CRS (nonpartisan), 2024 edition of the TANF FAQ report. Benefit data in the report are from July 2022 (a family of two received from $915 a month in New Hampshire to $162 in Arkansas). TANF phase-out rules (earned income disregards) vary by state; the Urban Institute's Welfare Rules Database is the state-by-state source (not saved; evidence still needed).

statement: The 2026 federal poverty guideline for the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia is $15,960 for one person, $27,320 for three and $33,000 for four.
anchor:
2026 POVERTY GUIDELINES FOR THE 48 CONTIGUOUS STATES AND THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA
Persons in family/household Poverty guideline
1 $15,960
2 $21,640
3 $27,320
4 $33,000
5 $38,680
6 $44,360
7 $50,040

context: HHS ASPE, second Trump administration. The 2026 guidelines compare 11 months of 2025 CPI-U with 2024 because of the October 2025 shutdown (ASPE note). Premium tax credits for 2026 use the guidelines published in early 2025, not these (KFF reports $62,600 as the 2026 single-person 400 percent line, which is 400 percent of $15,650).

statement: ASPE lists SNAP, the National School Lunch Program, LIHEAP, Head Start and the Children's Health Insurance Program among programs using the poverty guidelines or multiples of them (for instance 125 or 185 percent), and says TANF, SSI and the earned income credit do not use them.
anchor: Programs using the guidelines (or percentage multiples of the guidelines — for instance, 125 percent or 185 percent of the guidelines) in determining eligibility include Head Start, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), the National School Lunch Program, the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, and the Children’s Health Insurance Program.

Note that in general, cash public assistance programs (Temporary Assistance for Needy Families and Supplemental Security Income) do NOT use the poverty guidelines in determining eligibility. The Earned Income Tax Credit program also does NOT use the poverty guidelines to determine eligibility.
context: HHS ASPE, second Trump administration, plain description. Housing uses area median income (EV-SEC-512), CCDF state median income (EV-SEC-530), the tax credits tax filing units.

statement: Under the tax code's refund-disregard rule any refund, or advance payment of a refundable credit, made to an individual under the tax code is not income, and not a resource for 12 months, in determining eligibility or benefit amounts under any federal program or any state or local program financed in whole or in part with federal funds.
anchor: Notwithstanding any other provision of law, any refund (or advance payment with respect to a refundable credit) made to any individual under this title shall not be taken into account as income, and shall not be taken into account as resources for a period of 12 months from receipt, for purposes of determining the eligibility of such individual (or any other individual) for benefits or assistance (or the amount or extent of benefits or assistance) under any Federal program or under any State or local program financed in whole or in part with Federal funds.
context: The statute (2024 edition). It is why a refundable child benefit paid through the tax system does not raise rent or reduce SNAP (dossiers/shared-rules.md, rule 1). A benefit paid outside the tax code has no such protection unless its own statute says so.

statement: CRS states that there is no uniform definition of modified adjusted gross income; the term has different definitions depending on the purpose for which it is being calculated.
anchor: There is no uniform definition of MAGI; rather, the term has different definitions depending on the purpose for which it is being calculated.
context: CRS (nonpartisan), R43861 (2016). Older report; the tax-code definitions it compares have been amended since (for example for the senior deduction, EV-SEC-505, which defines its own MAGI).

statement: CRS reported that Supplemental Security Income and Veterans Affairs benefits use income definitions which include most sources of income, taxable and nontaxable, while Medicaid and the premium credit use a tax-based MAGI definition.
anchor: which include most sources of income, taxable and nontaxable, when determining eligibility.
most other low-income programs include other types of income (e.g., nontaxable pensions) and asset holdings that are also exc
locator: Definitions of Income Used in Selected Low-Income Programs
context: CRS (nonpartisan), R41997 (2011-2013 versions). Only a 2011-2013 CRS comparison table was found; no current CRS or GAO report comparing income definitions across federal programs was found (evidence still needed). Its second quotation is cut off at the saved text's own line wrap.

statement: CBO estimated that in 2016, counting federal payroll taxes, state income taxes and the phase-out of SNAP and cost-sharing subsidies, only 16 percent of low- and moderate-income taxpayers would face a marginal tax rate between 10 and 19 percent and 78 percent a higher rate, against 48 percent and 23 percent under the federal income tax alone; more than half would face 20 to 39 percent.
anchor: CBO estimates that in 2016, about 48 percent of low- and moderate-income taxpayers under age 65 with earnings will face a marginal tax rate between 10 percent and 19 percent under the federal income tax system, and 23 percent will face a higher rate
Only 16 percent of taxpayers will face marginal tax rates between 10 percent and 19 percent, and 78 percent will face higher rates.
More than half will face marginal tax rates between 20 percent and 39 percent.
context: CBO (nonpartisan), November 2015; tax-return simulation of workers under 450 percent of poverty. It includes SNAP and the ACA cost-sharing subsidies but not housing assistance or TANF, so it understates the stack for assisted families. It does not report the share above 50 or 60 percent in the text read; the distribution above 50 percent, and the CBO 2012 report (pub. 43709), are evidence still needed.

statement: CBO's hypothetical single parent with one child in Pennsylvania faced marginal tax rates averaging 75 percent over a narrow range of income (115 to 126 percent of poverty), from the combined phase-out of the earned income credit and SNAP, the 10 percent income tax bracket and the 15.3 percent payroll tax.
anchor: The combination of the phaseout of the EITC and SNAP benefits, the 10 percent federal income tax bracket, and the 15.3 percent federal payroll tax causes a sharp increase in marginal tax rates, which average 75 percent over a narrow range of income (from 115 percent to 126 percent of the FPL).
context: CBO (nonpartisan), November 2015; a stylized family receiving TANF, SNAP, Medicaid/CHIP and cost-sharing subsidies, 2016 law (pre-2017 tax law, ACA 400 percent cliff). CBO says it "is not indicative of the distribution". Pennsylvania chosen as typical of state income taxes.

statement: CBO estimated that 62 percent of lower-income families did not receive means-tested transfers in 2013, and of those who did, most participated in only one program.
anchor: An estimated 62 percent of lower-income families did not receive those means-tested transfers in 2013, either because they did not meet additional nonfinancial requirements or because they were eligible but did not apply for benefits. Of those who received transfers, most participated in only one program.
context: CBO (nonpartisan), November 2015, from the 2014 CPS ASEC; transfers were TANF, SNAP, Medicaid, CHIP and cost-sharing subsidies. This is why CBO's average (31 percent, EV-HOU-401) is far below the stacked examples.

statement: HHS ASPE simulated that among households with children just above poverty the median marginal tax rate after a $2,000 earnings increase is 51 percent, never below 42 percent up to 200 percent of poverty, and that about three million households with children below 200 percent of poverty receiving SNAP, the earned income credit, the child tax credit and Medicaid/CHIP have a median rate of 42 percent.
anchor:
Among households with children, when earnings increase by $2,000 (see Figure
1, dark red line), median marginal tax rates rise precipitously from negative 22
percent 1 (when family income is 24 percent of poverty or less) to 51 percent
(when family income is just above poverty).

rates remain high (never dipping below 42
percent) as incomes approach 200 percent of poverty.

Among households with children below 200 percent of poverty, the most
common combination of benefits is SNAP + EITC + Child Tax Credits (CTC)
+ Medicaid/Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP), and these three
million households experience a median marginal tax rate of 42 percent.
context: HHS ASPE (Chien and Macartney), March 2019, first Trump administration; TRIM3 microsimulation on the 2015 CPS ASEC; a $2,000 earnings increase from federal and state taxes and transfers. Agency analysis, treated with the usual skepticism; the series page defines a cliff as a benefit reduction equal to or larger than the earnings increase.

statement: Maag, Steuerle, Chakravarti and Quakenbush found that a single parent with two children whose wages rise from the poverty level to 150 percent of poverty can face a marginal tax rate between 26.6 percent and over 100 percent depending on the state, and that the rate varies sharply with earnings pattern and program participation.
anchor: A single parent with two children who increases her wages from poverty-level to 150 percent of poverty-level can face a tax rate between 26.6 percent and over 100 percent, depending on which state she lives in.
This paper shows how sensitive marginal tax rates are to assumptions about state of residence, earning patterns, and program participation.
context: Urban Institute and Tax Policy Center researchers; peer reviewed (National Tax Journal 65(4), December 2012); a simulation of a family across states under 2012 law. Authors warn the rates may overstate what families face because they assume income is earned evenly through the year.

statement: Using the 2019 Survey of Consumer Finances and a life-cycle model, Altig and co-authors found that over half of working-age Americans face lifetime marginal net tax rates above 40 percent, one in four households in the bottom lifetime resource quintile above 50 percent, and one in ten above 70 percent.
anchor: We use TFA in conjunction with the 2019 Survey of Consumer Finances to calculate Americans’ remaining lifetime marginal net tax rates (LMTR).
Over half of working-age Americans face LMTRs exceeding 40 percent. One in four households in the bottom lifetime resource quintile face LMTRs above 50 percent. One in ten face rates above 70 percent
context: NBER working paper 27164 (2020, revised 2023); not peer reviewed. Funded by the Sloan Foundation, the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta and the Goodman Institute; Kotlikoff owns the firm whose engine is used (disclosed). Model-based, includes lifetime effects (benefits and taxes over the life cycle), so not directly comparable with current-year rates.

statement: In the Atlanta Fed's illustration of a hypothetical single mother with two children in Clarke County, Georgia, moving from concessions worker to certified nursing assistant lowers net resources by more than $11,000 over three years, and from nursing assistant to licensed practical nurse by more than $35,000, which the page attributes to reduced work hours while in school and benefits cliffs; over a lifetime both moves pay.
anchor: The chart above demonstrates an example of benefits cliffs for a hypothetical single mother with two children who lives in Clarke County, Georgia.
Leia's cumulatively experiences a decline of more than $11,000.
Leia would suffer a loss of net financial resources exceeding $35,000 during the first three years of the transition.
These declines are the results of reduced work hours while in school and the prevalence of benefits cliffs.
When resources are calculated over a lifetime, however, both scenarios would deliver a positive return
locator: What Are Benefits Cliffs?, Leia example
context: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta (central-bank research arm; promotes its CLIFF tools), undated web page; a worked example from its Policy Rules Database/CLIFF model, not a measured sample. The page does not break the loss down by program; the Ilin and Sanchez paper on mitigating cliffs was not found (evidence still needed).

statement: PolicyEngine simulated a Texas couple's premium tax credit: at 400% of poverty they are ineligible under the law after the enhanced credits expire, and would gain $2,899 a year had the enhanced credits been extended, which produces an infinite marginal rate at the cliff.
anchor: the Texas couple would gain $2,899 in annual credits at 400% FPL
a positive infinite MTR at 400% FPL under current law, where they become ineligible for the PTC
context: PolicyEngine (nonprofit open-source microsimulation), September 30, 2025, before the enhanced credits expired; archetype households, 2026 values. An "infinite" rate is the arithmetic of a cliff (loss of credit over a $1 rise). Not independently validated here.

statement: Under SSDI rules in 2019, beneficiaries who engaged in substantial gainful activity (earnings of $1,220 a month for most) for more than a year had their entire benefit suspended, creating a "cash cliff".
anchor: Under current SSDI rules, when beneficiaries engage in substantial gainful activity (SGA—defined as earnings of $1,220 per month for most SSDI beneficiaries) for more than a year, SSA suspends their entire benefit payment. This rule creates a “cash cliff” at the SGA threshold
context: Abt Global brief on the SSA-funded BOND trial, 2019; a description of the rule then in force, not a result. The 2026 amount is $1,690 (EV-SEC-525).

statement: In BOND, a randomized test run for SSA of a $1-for-$2 benefit offset on SSDI earnings above the annual equivalent of the substantial gainful activity amount, the evaluation found no statistically significant impact on average earnings in either stage, though the offset raised the share of beneficiaries with earnings above that amount by 7 percent in Stage 1 and 23 percent in Stage 2.
anchor: BOND tested a $1 for $2 benefit offset applied to annual earnings above the BOND Yearly Amount (BYA)

The evaluation found no statistically significant evidence of an impact of the benefit offset policy on average earnings either in the nationally representative Stage 1 sample or in the Stage 2 sample of volunteers.
the evaluation finds evidence in both stages that the benefit offset increased the share of beneficiaries with earnings above BYA—by 7 percent in Stage 1 and by 23 percent in Stage 2
context: Randomized trial run for SSA by Abt Associates with Mathematica; Stage 1 randomized 968,530 SSDI beneficiaries (2011 to 2015), Stage 2 12,744 volunteers; Abt brief of 2019 on the 2018 final report. The 7 and 23 percent are relative increases over the control mean, not percentage points.

statement: BOND also found the offset raised average SSDI benefits by $143 a year in Stage 1, and that 3.6 percent of the Stage 1 treatment group earned enough to trigger the offset in at least one year, against about 15 percent of the treatment groups in the volunteer sample.
anchor: In the nationally representative Stage 1 sample, the benefit offset increased average SSDI benefits by $143 per year (or about $12 per month) during the five year period.
Of the Stage 1 sample, 3.6 percent of the treatment group earned enough to trigger the offset, resulting in a reduction in their benefits, in at least one year during the follow-up period
About 15 percent of the treatment groups earned enough to trigger partial benefit payments in any year during the follow-up period
context: Same trial as EV-SEC-546. Two forces raised benefits: partial benefits to people who already earned above the line, and some of them cutting earnings. Most who triggered the offset would have earned that much anyway.

statement: SSA's BOND page reports that use of the benefit offset was modest, enhanced counseling had the same effect as regular counseling, and a benefit-cost analysis showed the total cost of the offset exceeded its total benefit.
anchor: The use of the benefit offset was modest, and enhanced counseling services had the same effect as regular counseling services. A benefit-cost analysis showed that the total cost of the benefit offset exceeded its total benefit.
context: SSA (second Trump administration, 2026 summary page) of the trial it commissioned. Same trial as the Abt brief, so corroboration of method but from a different publisher; the page's summary is the agency's.

statement: Saez found clear bunching around the first kink of the earned income credit concentrated solely among the self-employed, and no bunching at any other kink of the income tax schedule apart from the first bracket threshold.
anchor: We find clear evidence of bunching around the first kink point of the Earned Income Tax Credit but concentrated solely among the self-employed.
We find evidence of bunching at the threshold of the first income tax bracket where tax liability starts but no evidence of bunching at any other kink point.
context: Peer reviewed (American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, August 2010); US tax-return data; observational, not experimental. Bunching at a kink is evidence about reported income, which can reflect reporting rather than hours worked.

statement: Census Bureau researchers found that bunching around the poverty-line notch where premium tax credits start, in states that did not expand Medicaid, occurs only among filers with self-employment income, and found no evidence that wage and salary workers adjust their labor supply in response to the new subsidy.
anchor: bunching occurs only among ﬁlers with self-employment income.

no evidence that wage and salary workers adjust their labor supply in response to increased availability
of directly purchased health insurance.
context: Kucko, Rinz and Solow, Census CARRA working paper 2017-07; not peer reviewed; tax records for the universe of returns, 2014 onward. The "100 percent" appears in the abstract's description of the notch.

statement: Using IRS data, Heim and co-authors found bunching of taxpayer incomes below 400% of poverty in 2014 that is only apparent among marketplace purchasers who could get the subsidy, among both self-employed and wage and salary workers, and primarily through increased IRA contributions.
anchor: We find a significant amount of bunching below 400% FPL in 2014 that is only apparent among those who purchased insurance from a marketplace
We see evidence of bunching at the cliff both among the self-employed and among wage and salary workers.
the bunching appears to primarily have been driven by increases in contributions to IRA accounts
context: Conference abstract (ASHEcon 2016) by Treasury-affiliated and Indiana University authors; the paper was later published in the Journal of Health Economics (2020), where the authors describe the overall amount of bunching as modest. IRS tax returns 2013 and 2014 (a difference-in-differences against 2013, when no subsidy existed). Shares authors with EV-SEC-552.

statement: Treasury-affiliated researchers estimated that around 85,000 taxpayers likely to have bought exchange insurance had income between 390% and 410% of poverty; close to 40% of them faced a cliff smaller than $100, though over 30% faced one above $3000.
anchor: We also estimate that around 85,000 taxpayers who were likely to have purchased insurance in an exchange had MAGI between 390% and 410% of FPL.
Close to 40% of these will face a cliff smaller than $100, though over 30% will face a cliff in excess of $3000.
context: National Tax Association proceedings, October 2014; tax data for 2011-2012 matched to exchange premiums, simulating 2014 rules; authors shared with EV-SEC-551. The authors note a larger cliff would exist if premiums rise faster than incomes. Under the 2026 schedule the credit is larger than in 2014 for many (premiums have risen), so cliff sizes are likely bigger now (judgment, not measured).

statement: Moffitt records that the AFDC benefit-reduction rate was 100 percent from 1935 to the 1967 Social Security Amendments, which lowered it to 67 percent, and that the 1981 Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act raised it back to 100 percent.
anchor: From 1935, when the Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC) program was enacted, to the 1967 Social Security Amendments, the tax rate in the program was 100 percent-that is, benefits were reduced by one dollar for every extra dollar earned. With the 1967 Amendments, Congress lowered the tax rate to 67 percent
Welfare reform was finally achieved in 1981 when the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (OBRA) was enacted.
But OBRA increased the tax rate back to 100 percent, the level prevailing prior to 1967.
context: Peer-reviewed conference paper (American Economic Review Papers and Proceedings, 1986) by Robert Moffitt. A historical account of the "30 and a third" disregard the 1967 amendments created and the 1981 law removed.

statement: Moffitt and Wolf found that the 1981 Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act hit working AFDC recipients hard, raising the implicit tax rate in the program to 78 percent, mainly by eliminating the "30-and-one-third" deduction.
anchor: The 1981 Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (OBRA) altered the Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC) program in important ways
We find that working recipients were very hard hit and that the "tax rate" implicit in the program rose to 78 percent.
the elimination of the "30-and-one-third" deduction was most important in raising the tax rate.
context: Peer reviewed (Social Service Review, June 1987); data on AFDC recipients active just before the 1981 law; simulates the effect on the benefit formula, not on observed hours. Shares an author with EV-SEC-553, so not independent corroboration of it. The paper measures the incentive change; the labor-supply effect is Moffitt's econometric estimate in EV-SEC-553's source (not quoted here).

statement: In November 2021 the UK government cut the Universal Credit taper rate from 63% to 55% and raised work allowances by £500 a year.
anchor: Work allowances, the amount a claimant can earn before their Universal Credit is reduced, will increase by £500 per year from today
the taper rate, the amount that a person’s Universal Credit is reduced by when their earnings are more than their work allowance, will drop from 63% to 55%.
context: UK Department for Work and Pensions press release, November 24, 2021 (Conservative government). Universal Credit replaced six means-tested benefits (Jobseeker's Allowance, Income Support, Housing Benefit, Employment and Support Allowance, Working Tax Credit, Child Tax Credit) with one payment and one taper. The taper applies to net earnings above a work allowance for households with a child or limited capability for work; others have none.

statement: The UK National Audit Office concluded in 2018 that Universal Credit was not value for money then and its future value for money was unproven, and that it doubted the Department could ever measure whether the aim of increasing employment had been achieved.
anchor: cause us to conclude that the project is not value for money now, and that its future value for money is unproven.
Both we, and the Department, doubt it will ever be possible for the Department to measure whether the economic goal of increasing employment has been achieved.
context: UK National Audit Office (independent public auditor), June 2018; a value-for-money audit of the rollout (delivery, costs, claimant hardship), not of the taper design. The five-week wait for a first payment and the effect of the 63 to 55 percent cut on work are not covered here (an IFS or Resolution Foundation analysis is evidence still needed).

statement: For the Canada Child Benefit payments of July 2026 onward, the benefit is reduced by 7% of adjusted family net income between $38,237 and $82,847 for one child, 13.5% for two, 19% for three and 23% for four or more; above $82,847 the reduction is a fixed amount plus 3.2% of income above that line for one child.
anchor: These amounts start being reduced when the adjusted family net income (AFNI) is over $38,237.
the reduction is 7% of the amount of AFNI greater than $38,237 up to $82,847
the reduction is 13.5% of the amount of AFNI greater than $38,237 up to $82,847
the reduction is 19% of the amount of AFNI greater than $38,237 up to $82,847
the reduction is 23% of the amount of AFNI greater than $38,237 up to $82,847
for income greater than $82,847, the reduction is $3,123 plus 3.2% of AFNI greater than $82,847
locator: How much you can expect to receive
context: Canada Revenue Agency (Canadian federal government), publication T4114 for the July 2026 to June 2027 payment year. The rates rise with the number of children, so the marginal rate is a function of family size; the phase-out is a single smooth schedule on one income measure.

statement: Canada Child Benefit entitlement is based on adjusted family net income for the calendar year before the benefit year, which in most cases equals net income on the tax return (the sum of both spouses' in a two-parent family).
anchor: In most cases, the AFNI is equal to the parent's net income as reported on the tax return in a one-parent family and to the sum of both spouses/common-law partners' net income in a two-parent family.
the CCB entitlement based on the adjusted family net income (AFNI) for the calendar year before the beginning of the benefit year
context: Department of Finance Canada, Report on Federal Tax Expenditures 2026. One income test from the tax return, run once a year, with payment monthly. Contrast with US programs that each re-verify income on their own cycle.

statement: Australia's Family Tax Benefit Part A is reduced by 20 cents per dollar of family adjusted taxable income over $69,131 (down to a base rate) and by 30 cents per dollar over $123,078 until it reaches nil.
anchor: This test reduces your FTB Part A by 20 cents for each dollar of income over $69,131.
We’ll reduce the rate of FTB Part A by 30 cents for each dollar of income over $123,078.
context: Services Australia (Australian federal government), page updated July 1, 2026. Income is "adjusted taxable income" from the tax system; payments can be reconciled after the tax return, which can cause overpayments.

statement: Under the transitional benefits alternative, a state that elects it freezes a household's SNAP allotment for up to 5 months after it leaves TANF, MOE or state-funded cash assistance, after adjusting for the loss of that income.
anchor: a State agency that has elected this option shall freeze the household's benefit allotment for up to 5 months after making an adjustment for the loss of TANF, MOE, or the SFCA.
context: 7 CFR 273.27(a) (eCFR, November 2026). State option.

statement: USDA's 2024 state options report counts 24 states and territories offering the transitional benefits alternative and 29 not offering it.
anchor: Benefits can be continued for up to 5 months at a level equal to the amount the household received prior to TANF termination
No TBA (29)
TBA (24)
context: USDA FNS, 16th State Options Report (June 2024, Biden administration); counts include Guam and the Virgin Islands. Later editions are not saved.

statement: GAO reported that under express lane eligibility a state Medicaid or CHIP agency may rely on another agency's findings (such as SNAP's income finding) even if that agency uses a different method, and that the option may be used only for children, not parents or other adults.
anchor: Under ELE, a state Medicaid or CHIP agency may rely on an Express Lane Agency’s findings even if the Express Lane Agency uses a different method than Medicaid or CHIP to derive those findings.
Under CHIPRA, the ELE option may only be used for Medicaid and CHIP eligibility determinations for children and cannot be used for parents or other adults.
context: GAO-13-178R (December 2012), nonpartisan legislative branch; describes the 2009 CHIPRA option. Children may be found eligible but not denied by ELE. Which states use it today, and its effects on enrollment, are not saved (CMS page blocks agents; evidence still needed).

statement: Colorado's Cliff Effect Pilot Program, authorized in 2012 in 15 counties, keeps families on child care assistance above the entry limit (statewide limit 165% of poverty; the program serves about 13% of eligible families); a 2019 evaluation presentation reported anecdotal evidence of greater economic mobility and recommended linking copay increases to income rises.
anchor: Authorized in 2012
15 counties
Statewide income eligibility: 165% FPL
Program only serves about 13% of eligible families
Families welcome assistance from CEPP, anecdotal evidence it enables greater economic mobility.
CEPP should link copay increases with household income increases
locator: slides: CCCAP Overview, Findings and Recommendations
context: Presentation by Colorado researchers to the National Governors Association, 2019; interviews and county data, no comparison group. The state pilot was the first of its kind; the evaluation says it is not well publicized. Later Colorado cliff measures (House Bill 1259 on TANF disregards) are not saved.

statement: The Tax Policy Center estimated that phasing in the child tax credit from the first dollar of earnings and allowing the full $2,000 to be refundable would cost about $48.5 billion over FY2025 to FY2034.
anchor: allowing the full $2,000 to be received as a refundable credit would cost about $48.5 billion over the 10-year budget window from FY2025 to FY2034 (Table 1).
locator: TaxVox post, paragraph on phasing in the CTC faster
context: Tax Policy Center, May 2025, written before the $2,200 law passed, so the baseline is a $2,000 credit; stance neutral. Headline matches the number, but it is the cost of a faster phase-in with the existing $2,000 cap, not of the full-refundability design with no earnings requirement, and it is not scaled to $2,200.

statement: Columbia's Center on Poverty and Social Policy estimated that 19 million children, 28 percent of those under 17, are ineligible for the full credit in 2025 because family income is too low, which is the group a fully refundable credit would reach.
anchor: We estimate that in 2025, more than 1 in 4 children (28%) under age 17 will be ineligible for the full Child Tax Credit under OBBBA because their family income is not high enough to qualify.

This represents 19 million children left behind: 17 million children previously ineligible for the full credit who see no gains under OBBBA and remain ineligible for the full credit plus roughly two million children in moderate-income families newly ineligible for the full credit.
context: Columbia University Center on Poverty and Social Policy, updated August 2025 for the final law; research center that favors a fully refundable credit. Counts the affected children, it does not score cost or poverty.

statement: The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities said that making the full $2,200 credit available to children in lower-income families would reduce the number of children below the poverty line by 1.2 million this year.
anchor: Making the full $2,200 credit available to families with lower incomes would have a meaningful impact on child poverty, reducing the number of children in families with incomes below the poverty line by 1.2 million this year.
locator: Section 'Policymakers Should Help Improve Economic Security'
context: Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, July 30, 2026; advocacy-oriented think tank. The estimate is attributed to a footnote not opened by this reader and the page does not state the poverty measure or the cost; treat as a secondary citation.

statement: The Century Foundation's simulation found that making the existing child tax credit fully refundable could cut the child poverty rate by 22 percent at about $23 billion per year.
anchor: making the existing Child Tax Credit fully refundable (as described in the Economic Mobility Act) could cut the child poverty rate by 22 percent.
making the existing Child Tax Credit fully refundable is estimated to cost $23 billion per year.
context: The Century Foundation, July 2020, by academics at Columbia and Toronto/Waterloo; pre-2021 law with a $2,000 credit, financing not modeled. The cost is annual in 2020 dollars and the credit amount is below today's $2,200, so scale it up before comparing.

statement: The Century Foundation modeled a Canada-style child benefit with no phase-in that would cut U.S. child poverty from 13.5 percent to 6.4 percent, moving 5.3 million children out of poverty, at $50 billion to $80 billion per year on top of the existing credit.
anchor: The results show that a credit modeled on the Canada Child Benefit would reduce the child poverty rate by more than half (from 13.5 percent to 6.4 percent)
This translates to 5.3 million children overall and 1.6 million young children being moved out of poverty.
a child allowance in the United States similar to the Canada Child Benefit would cost between $50 billion and $80 billion per year (on top of the existing costs of the Child Tax Credit)
locator: Figure 3, Table 2 text and cost paragraph
context: The Century Foundation, July 2020. Design: up to $4,803 per young child and $4,053 per older child, full benefit below $22,095, then phased out (2020 dollars). The paper itself says financing and labor-force effects are not modeled. Headline matches its numbers.

statement: The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimated that replacing the child tax credit with a Canada-style child benefit would cut the number of poor children by more than half, at about $50 billion to $80 billion a year more than the credit it replaces.
anchor: Transforming the CTC into a child benefit resembling the CCB would reduce the number of children under age 18 living in poverty by more than half, we estimate
it would cost about $50 billion to $80 billion a year more than the CTC it would replace.
context: Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, May 2018, by Arloc Sherman; progressive-leaning think tank. Uses 2015 CPS data with TRIM3 corrections in 2018 dollars. Its cost range matches the Century Foundation's, partly because the same academic literature informs both.

statement: CRFB reported that CBO estimated making the American Rescue Plan child tax credit expansion permanent at $1.60 trillion, while CRFB's own model gave $1.19 trillion, with the gap attributed to methodology.
anchor: | Expand the CTC | $1.60 trillion* | $1.19 trillion* |
*Differences on Child Tax Credit and SALT are largely due to methodological differences.
locator: Table 'Comparison of Estimated Cost of Permanent Build Back Better Act'
context: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, December 10, 2021, reporting a CBO/JCT letter to the Budget Committee ranking members. The CBO figure covers the Build Back Better version of the credit (ARPA amounts, refundable) over 2022-2031; CRFB assumes the TCJA is extended separately, which lowers its number.

statement: The Peter G. Peterson Foundation summarized CBO as estimating that making the ARPA child credit expansions permanent would cost $1.6 trillion over 2022-2031.
anchor: If those expansions were to become permanent, CBO estimates that they would cost $1.6 trillion over the 2022-2031 period.
context: Peter G. Peterson Foundation, February 2022; a secondary summary of CBO. Same CBO number as in the CRFB table, so not independent of it. Pre-dates the 2025 law, so the current-law baseline differs.

statement: The Tax Foundation estimated that making the ARPA expanded child tax credit permanent would cost $1.6 trillion over the 10-year budget window on a conventional basis.
anchor: permanent would cost $1.6 trillion on a conventional basis over the 10-year budget window using a current law baseline.
context: Tax Foundation, March 19, 2021; market-oriented think tank, own general equilibrium model. Independent of CBO; lands at the same $1,557.8 billion-scale figure.

statement: The Congressional Research Service reported that the Joint Committee on Taxation estimated a permanent extension of the American Rescue Plan childless EITC expansion would cost $135 billion over FY2022-FY2031, versus $13 billion for a one-year extension.
anchor: The Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT) estimated that a permanent extension of these changes would cost $135 billion over a 10-year budgetary window (FY2022-FY2031).
JCT estimated a temporary one-year extension of these changes would cost $13 billion over the same time period
context: Congressional Research Service In Focus, December 13, 2021, relaying a Joint Committee on Taxation score; nonpartisan. The score covers the ARPA childless EITC design made permanent over 2022-2031 and the baseline is pre-2025 law.

statement: The Tax Policy Center estimated that restoring the 2021 childless EITC would cost $14.0 billion in fiscal year 2026 and $135.4 billion over FY2025-34, before any marriage-penalty relief.
anchor: Restoring the 2021 childless EITC with no other changes would cost $14.0 billion in fiscal year 2026.
context: Tax Policy Center, April 2025 (date taken from the file path); table sources are TPC Table T25-0105 and JCT Table 25-0-026. Same cost scale as the 2021 JCT score, which supports it. The ten-year figure is read from a flattened table row, so check the column against the PDF before quoting it.

statement: CRFB estimated that permanently extending the ARPA child and dependent care credit expansion would cost $90 billion over ten years in total, including $10 billion for the ARPA year itself.
anchor: | Permanently extend child and dependent care credit expansion | $10 billion | $80 billion | $90 billion |
locator: Table 'Ten-Year Cost of American Rescue Plan Act With Extensions'
context: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, March 5, 2021; CRFB calculations from CBO data, deficit-focused. The 2021 design is a 50 percent rate on up to $8,000 of expenses per child, fully refundable. Pre-dates 2025 law. No JCT/CBO score of a permanent refundable version was found by this reader.

statement: The Joint Economic Committee estimated that over 9.1 million families were eligible for the 2021 expanded and fully refundable child and dependent care credit, with an average credit of $2,244, compared with 6.5 million families who claimed it before.
anchor: According to estimates from the Joint Economic Committee, more than 9.1 million families were eligible for the expanded Child and Dependent Care Tax Credit in 2021 and could claim the credit as part of their tax return. Before the expansion, just 6.5 million families claimed the credit.
Nationally, families were eligible for an average credit of $2,244, reimbursing 39% of child care expenses thanks to the Rescue Plan.
locator: Page 1, 'The American Rescue Plan made 9.1 million families eligible'
context: Joint Economic Committee staff brief under the Democratic majority in 2021, so advocacy-leaning; eligibility estimate, not claims data and not a cost score. Says the credit was made fully refundable for the first time, which is who gains: low-income families who had no tax to offset.

statement: Brookings said the earlier child and dependent care credit was nonrefundable, did not benefit the lowest-income families, and was heavily skewed toward families making more than $100,000 a year.
anchor: The CDCTC provides tax credits to families for a portion of their child care expenses. However, it is nonrefundable and thus does not benefit Americans with the lowest incomes. In fact, its benefits are heavily skewed toward families making more than $100,000 a year.
context: Brookings Institution, May 27, 2021, by Isabel Sawhill and Morgan Welch; centrist think tank. A characterization of the credit's distribution with no table in the extract; use alongside a distributional table from TPC or JCT.

statement: The Niskanen Center estimated that the Family Security Act 2.0 would lift over 1.1 million children out of poverty, a 12.6 percent reduction in the child poverty rate.
anchor: The net impact of the Family Security Act 2.0 would be to lift over 1.1 million children out of poverty, a 12.6 percent reduction in the child poverty rate.
context: Niskanen Center, June 15, 2022, by Robert Orr; center-right think tank that is generally positive toward the plan. SPM, 2020 CPS data. Close to the Tax Policy Center and Urban figure for the same plan, from a different model.

statement: The Tax Policy Center and Urban Institute estimated that Family Security Act 2.0 would cut child poverty from 14 percent to 12.4 percent and cost just under $45 billion per year, against about $100 billion for the expanded child tax credit.
anchor: We estimate that FSA 2.0, had it been in place in 2018, would lift over 1.2 million children out of poverty and reduce the child poverty rate from 14 percent to 12.4 percent (table 1).
We estimate that FSA 2.0 would cost just under $45 billion per year, while the expanded CTC would cost around $100 billion per year (both estimates are in 2018 dollars).
context: Tax Policy Center, December 2022, by Werner, Airi and Maag using the Urban Institute ATTIS model on 2018 data; nonpartisan. The authors warn the cost may not match other models, especially the savings from offsets. Poverty effect is similar to Niskanen's 12.6 percent.

statement: SSA's Office of the Chief Actuary estimated that raising the SSI resource limits to $10,000 and $20,000 and indexing them would raise federal SSI payments by $8.9 billion over 2025 through 2034.
anchor: we estimate the increase in Federal SSI payments would be $8.9 billion over the calendar year period 2025 through 2034
unmarried individuals and $3,000 for married couples to $10,000 for unmarried individuals and
$20,000 for married couples, and would index these resource limits by the annual percentage
context: SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, 7 August 2026, answering Senator Cassidy; estimate is for a proposal similar to S. 1234 with a 2027 start, assuming indexing from 2028. The headline cost is small because the cost grows from $0.5 billion in 2027 to $1.4 billion in 2034 (the table I read); no trust-fund effect stated.

statement: The Roosevelt Institute's microsimulation estimated that the SSI Restoration Act of 2024, which sets the maximum benefit at the poverty line for one person, would cost about $61 billion a year in 2024 dollars, almost doubling SSI spending.
anchor: We find that the SSI Restoration Act of 2024 would cost about $61 billion annually in real 2024 dollars.
the SSI Restoration Act would almost double annual expenditures on SSI
sets the maximum benefit for a single recipient to the Federal Poverty Line for a household of one
context: Roosevelt Institute (progressive think tank), Stephen Nuñez, 5 February 2026; preview of a March 2026 report; not an official score. The post says the benefit increase alone is a preliminary estimate. It states SSA's own estimate for the 2021 version was in line with this figure.

statement: The Roosevelt Institute estimated that the SSI Restoration Act would add 2.58 million SSI recipient households and cut the SSI household poverty rate by 17.46 percentage points to 11.76 percent.
anchor: We estimate that the SSI Restoration Act would generate an additional 2.58 million SSI recipient households
The SSI household poverty rate would drop by 17.46 percentage points to 11.76 percent.
context: Same Roosevelt Institute microsimulation (2024 CPS ASEC, Supplemental Poverty Measure); the effect covers SSI households including newly eligible ones, not all poor people.

statement: Urban Institute estimated that the Senate-passed 2025 reconciliation bill's SNAP provisions would make 22.3 million families lose some or all benefits, with 5.3 million losing at least $25 a month, averaging $146 a month.
anchor: 22.3 million US families would be affected, losing some or all of their SNAP benefits.
Of the total affected families, 5.3 million would lose at least $25 in SNAP benefits per month.
Families losing at least $25 per month would lose $146 per month on average
context: Urban Institute, July 2025, preliminary; models the Senate-passed text fully in effect (not temporary Alaska and Hawaii exemptions). Every SNAP family counts as affected because of the Thrifty Food Plan indexing cap, so the 22.3 million headline overstates large losses; the 5.3 million figure is the better guide.

statement: Urban Institute estimated that the reconciliation law, counting direct effects and likely state responses, would raise the number of people in deep poverty by 3.4 million, including 0.8 million children.
anchor: We estimate that the number of people in deep poverty would rise by about a quarter, or 3.4 million, including an increase of 35 percent (0.8 million) for children.
context: Urban Institute, 29 October 2026. Covers the whole law (SNAP, Medicaid, tax changes) so it is the cost of not repealing it, not a SNAP-only figure; includes assumed state responses beyond the law's direct effects.

statement: A federal evaluation found Year Up services cost $27,158 per treatment group member, including $6,885 for stipends, and a net Year Up related cost of $23,135 per participant over seven years.
anchor: The cost of Year Up services was $27,158 per treatment group member (Exhibit 5-2, first panel).
This estimate includes $20,273 for staffing, facilities, and small payments to college partners and $6,885 for stipends.
and a difference (i.e., total Year Up related cost) of $23,135.
context: ACF OPRE with Abt Associates, April 2022, randomized trial; costs from program financial records. Year Up is at the high end of workforce programs, and employers pay for most of the internship cost, so the figure is not the public cost.

statement: Project QUEST participants in the randomized study received support for an average of 22 months at an average cost of $10,501 per participant.
anchor: Study participants received support from Project QUEST for an average of 22 months, and the average cost per participant was $10,501.
context: Economic Mobility Corporation, April 2017, a nonprofit evaluator; trial of health-care trainees in San Antonio. Cost is in dollars of the study period, not inflated to 2026.

statement: MDRC found WorkAdvance services cost between $6,400 and $8,300 per participant in 2018 dollars across the four providers.
anchor: WorkAdvance services cost between $6,400 and $8,300 per participant (in 2018 dollars) across the four providers
context: MDRC five-year report on a randomized trial; gross provider operating cost, not net of control-group services.

statement: The Department of Labor's program year 2026 allotment notice gives appropriated levels of $875,649,000 for WIOA Adult, $1,396,412,000 for Dislocated Worker (including the national reserve) and $948,130,000 for Youth.
anchor: The total appropriated funds for Adult Activities in PY 2026 is $875,649,000.
The amount appropriated for Dislocated Worker activities in PY 2026 totals $1,396,412,000.
The appropriated level for PY 2026 for WIOA Youth Activities totals $948,130,000.
locator: Federal Register notice, Adult, Dislocated Worker and Youth sections
context: DOL ETA, 28 April 2026. The Dislocated Worker figure includes the national reserve; the state formula share is smaller. Participants served were not in the pages I read.

statement: The Department of Labor reported that in program year 2023 Job Corps cost on average $49,769.53 per enrollee and $80,284.65 per student per year, and that participants earned $16,695 a year on average after leaving.
anchor: Average Cost Per Enrollee (Regardless of Length of Stay): $49,769.53
Average Cost Per Student Per Year (Average PY23 Headcount): $80,284.65
Job Corps participants earn $16,695 annually on average, post separation
locator: Release summary of the Transparency Report
context: DOL ETA, 25 April 2025; residential program costs are far above non-residential training. The release stresses inefficient centers; the earlier DOL estimate for program year 2017 was lower, so the cost trend is not comparable without checking method.

statement: DOL's American Apprenticeship Initiative evaluation found grantees spent $5,171 per registered apprentice by September 2021 (median grantee $6,407), and $8,802 per apprentice at smaller grantees against $3,876 at larger ones.
anchor: By the end of September 2021, total cost per apprentice was $5,171, but the median grantee spent about $6,407 per apprentice.
The weighted average cost for smaller grantees through September 2021 was $8,802, compared to $3,876 for larger grantees.
context: DOL evaluation, September 2022. This is grant spending to add apprentices, not the total cost of an apprenticeship; employer wages and training are separate, and the brief says pre-apprenticeship outlays may overstate the figure.

statement: Under the Inflation Reduction Act, apprentices must perform 15% of labor hours on clean-energy facilities that begin construction in 2024 or after (12.5% in 2023, 10% earlier), and any contractor with 4 or more workers must hire at least one qualified apprentice.
anchor: The applicable percentage is 10% for construction beginning before 2023, 12.5% for construction beginning in 2023, and 15% for construction beginning in 2024 or after.

any taxpayer, contractor, or subcontractor that employs 4 or more individuals at any time during the course of the construction, alteration, or repair of the facility must hire at least one qualified apprentice.
context: IRS guidance restating statute section 45(b)(8) and final regulations (June 2024); the labor hours test is also subject to the apprentice-to-journeyworker ratio.

statement: The IRS says taxpayers who meet the prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements can generally increase the base amounts of certain clean energy tax incentives by 5 times, with a good faith exception when no qualified apprentices are available.
anchor: taxpayers can generally increase the base amounts of certain clean energy tax incentives by 5 times.

A good faith effort exception may apply when a taxpayer, contractor, subcontractor has requested qualified apprentices from a registered apprenticeship program and no qualified apprentices are available.
context: IRS Publication 5855 (Rev. 6-2024). The exception means the apprenticeship requirement is soft where the apprentice supply is short, which limits its pull on demand for apprentices.

statement: A peer-reviewed evaluation of Oregon's highway construction program found pre-apprenticeship programs improved recruitment of women into the trades, and that non-financial support, supplies and child care services were each linked to higher apprenticeship completion.
anchor: We find pre-apprenticeship programs have improved the recruitment of women into the trades.

We further find that non-financial services, ready supplies, and childcare services have a positive impact on completion, with receipt of non-financial support having the largest impact on completion.
context: Peer-reviewed article (SAGE), March 2022; one state program, administrative data and interviews, not randomized, so completion effects may reflect who received services. I read only the abstract.

statement: In the PACE evaluation Year Up was the only program with ongoing stipends, up to $8,870 for the full year; 96 percent of its treatment group enrolled in training and 75 percent completed.
anchor: substantial financial stipends (of up to $8,870 for the full year)
fully 96 percent of treatment group members in the PACE Year Up evaluation enrolled in training and 75 percent completed the program.
Notably, no program other than Year Up offered stipends
context: ACF OPRE with Abt Associates, August 2021. The report suggests the conditional stipend may help completion, but the trial has no stipend versus no-stipend arm, so it does not isolate the stipend effect.

statement: A UK What Works Centre review of 11 studies concluded that payments to individuals or firms may increase participation in or completion of employment training, but effects on employment and earnings are less likely.
anchor: We found 11 studies that examined the effectiveness of financial incentives for employment training.
The evidence suggests that payments to either individuals or firms may increase participation in, or completion of, employment training, but that effects on employment and earnings are less likely.
locator: Section 'How effective are they?' and 'How secure is the evidence?'
context: What Works Centre for Local Economic Growth (UK), evidence review dated 2017 by file name; mostly UK and European trials, so transfer to US stipends is indirect. Supports the cautious reading of the Year Up completion figures.

statement: Urban Institute's microsimulation puts the benefit cost of the FAMILY Act at about 0.46 percent of taxable earnings, against a 0.40 percent payroll tax split between employees and employers.
anchor: The total estimated cost of benefits under the FAMILY Act is approximately 0.46 percent of total taxable earnings.
The FAMILY Act assesses a 0.40 percent payroll tax split evenly between employees and employers on uncapped earnings.
context: Urban Institute, September 2024, prepared under contract for the Department of Labor Women's Bureau; simulated as if implemented in 2018, with existing state programs accounted for. The headline matches its numbers: the rate it needs is slightly above the bill's 0.40 percent, the rest from general revenue per the bill. Urban does not claim a government score.

statement: Urban Institute estimates that under the FAMILY Act 4.9 percent of workers, about 8 million people, would take a covered leave, producing 9.2 million leaves and roughly $43 billion a year in benefit payments.
anchor: An estimated 4.9 percent of all workers, 8 million individuals, would take a covered paid leave, representing 9.2 million leaves taken in total and approximately $43 billion in annual benefit payments.
context: Urban Institute, September 2024, Department of Labor-funded. Take-up is modeled to replicate observed leave numbers in state programs, so a new national program with more awareness could exceed it; the report itself says it reflects 'modest take-up'. Dollar figures are 2018 levels.

statement: Urban Institute projects a higher share of the lowest earners (8.8 percent) than of the highest earners (2.5 percent) would receive FAMILY Act benefits, helped by a formula that replaces 85 percent of the first $1,257 of monthly earnings.
anchor: we project a higher share of these lowest earners would receive paid leave benefits (8.8 percent) than the highest earnings group (2.5 percent).
The plan would replace 85 percent of monthly earnings below $1,257, plus 69 percent of monthly earnings between $1,257 and $3,500, and 50 percent of monthly earnings between $3,500 and $6,200.
locator: Results by earnings group; policy description
context: Urban Institute, September 2024. A simulation of a progressive replacement formula, not an observed outcome; the same report notes that the lowest earners are less likely to be eligible at all because of the minimum earnings requirement, and that weekly dollar benefits remain higher for higher earners.

statement: Urban Institute estimates the FAMILY Act would cut the poverty rate by over 16 percent among people in families receiving benefits, and by 1 percent across the full population.
anchor: we estimate that the poverty rate would be reduced by over 16 percent among people in families receiving PFML benefits and by 1 percent across the full population.
context: Urban Institute, September 2024, using the Supplemental Poverty Measure. The 16 percent figure is relative (a share of the baseline rate) among benefit recipients only; across everyone the effect is one percent.

statement: IWPR estimated that the proposed FAMILY Act would cost less than half of one percent of taxable payroll.
figures: less than half of one percent
anchor: implementing the proposed Family and Medical Insurance Leave Act (FAMILY Act) would cost less than half of one percent of taxable payroll
context: Institute for Women's Policy Research, a nonprofit that supports paid leave; press release on the 25th anniversary of the FMLA, based on IWPR's own paid leave simulation model. No numbers beyond the range are on the page, and it describes the 2018 bill, not the 2023 or 2025 versions.

statement: A working paper notes that California raised its paid family leave wage replacement rate to about 60 to 70 percent, depending on income, in 2018.
anchor: In 2018, the wage replacement rate increased to approximately 60 to 70 percent (depending on income)
context: IZA Discussion Paper (Bailey, Byker, Patel, Ramnath, January 2024), a working paper that describes the law in a footnote. It is secondary to California's statute and EDD guidance; the rate is a description of enacted state law.

statement: An IZA working paper summarizing Bana, Bedard and Rossin-Slater reports that higher California wage replacement had little detectable effect on leave duration or short-term employment, but the design identifies the effect only for women at or above the 92nd percentile of earnings, so it says little about low earners.
anchor: increases in wage replacement have little detectable effect on leave duration or short-term employment, but the identification strategy recovers the causal effect of wage replacement only for very high earners in at least the 92nd percentile of the female wage distribution
context: Bailey and others, IZA discussion paper, January 2024, a secondhand summary of an earlier study; not itself an evaluation of the 2018 increase on low earners. It contests any reading that higher replacement shows no effect on low-earner take-up, because those earners fall outside the study's design.

statement: A Congressional Research Service report says the experimental CPI-E, built for people aged 62 and older, has greater sampling error than the official indexes, and uses the CPI-U's retail outlet sample, which may not match where older people shop.
anchor: an experimental price index to track changes in the cost of living for the population aged 62 and older.
The CPI-E therefore is subject to greater sampling error than the official indexes because of BLS’ limited resources.

The CPI-E also uses the CPI-U’s sample of retail outlets to gather prices, but the outlets may not accurately reflect those at which the elderly shop and the prices may not be representative of those paid by the elderly.
locator: Section on the experimental index, p. 5
context: Congressional Research Service, September 2011; a later CRS version exists (the register holds a 2015 CRS report at EV-SEC-440). This page does not mention senior discounts, so that point could not be confirmed from it. The CRS notes the gap with the CPI-W may partly reflect these limits.

statement: Penn Wharton Budget Model projects that the combined Social Security trust fund depletes in February 2035, after which payable benefits fall to 85 percent of scheduled benefits and decline to 60 percent by 2100.
anchor: PWBM projects that the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) trust fund depletes in February 2033 and that the combined OASI and Disability Insurance (OASDI) fund depletes in February 2035. At that point, payable benefits fall to 85 percent of scheduled benefits, declining to 60 percent by 2100
context: Penn Wharton Budget Model, University of Pennsylvania, September 2026. PWBM's own baseline, more pessimistic on dates than the Trustees (who show late 2034 for the combined fund and 83 percent payable); the page gives both for comparison.

statement: CRFB's summary of the Trustees' Report says the OASI trust fund is projected to be insolvent in 2032, bringing an automatic 22% benefit cut, and that the 75-year actuarial deficit is 4.42% of payroll.
anchor: The Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) trust fund is projected to be insolvent in 2032, when today’s youngest retirees turn 68, at which point retirees face an automatic 22% benefit cut.
Over the next 75 years, Social Security faces a 4.42% of payroll (1.5% of GDP) actuarial deficit
context: CRFB, June 9, 2026, relaying the Trustees' report; a nonpartisan but deficit-reduction-oriented group that calls for 'trust fund solutions'. The 22% cut applies to OASI alone; on a combined basis CRFB reports a 17% cut in 2034.

statement: Penn Wharton Budget Model scores a revenue-heavy option (payroll rate from 12.4 to 13.4 percent, taxable maximum $250,000, half-rate donut hole, chained CPI) as delaying OASI depletion to 2058, and finds none of five options fully restores solvency.
anchor: It combines a 1.0 percentage point increase in the OASI payroll tax rate (from 12.4 to 13.4 percent) with a higher taxable maximum ($250,000, up from $184,500 in 2026)
Option A delays depletion to 2058.
All five options, A through E, improve the long-range balance but none fully restores solvency
context: Penn Wharton Budget Model, March 2026. Option A is the most tax-heavy of five bundles, and the page itself notes that options which delay depletion most are the least effective at reducing the long-range imbalance. Dynamic model; not a CBO or SSA score.

statement: In a Penn Wharton Budget Model comparison of seven Social Security packages, all close roughly the same 75-year shortfall of 4.78 percent of taxable payroll; GDP in 2060 is 0.4 percent above baseline under the tax-only package and 12.1 percent above under the benefit-only package.
anchor: All seven packages approximately close a 75-year shortfall of 4.78 percent of taxable payroll and avoid depletion of the combined OASDI trust fund through 2100.
By 2060, GDP is 0.4 percent above baseline under Package A (“tax-only”) and 12.1 percent above baseline under Package F (“benefit-only”)
context: Penn Wharton Budget Model, September 2026. The growth gap is a model result driven by private saving responses and is sensitive to assumptions; the page also says every package produces losses for older current workers and near-retirees and gains for future households. Contrast with revenue-first views in the other register entries.

statement: Relaying a CBO report to Senator Hatch, CRFB says closing the 75-year shortfall through the payroll tax alone would take a 3.54 percentage point rate increase (to 15.94 percent), while eliminating the taxable maximum would close 45 percent of the gap.
anchor: Closing the 75-year shortfall through the payroll tax alone would require an immediate 3.54 percentage point increase in the payroll tax rate (to 15.94 percent)
eliminating the cap altogether would close 45 percent.
context: CRFB, July 14, 2014, summarizing a CBO report; the numbers are on CBO's 2014 baseline and are out of date, but they show the order of magnitude. I could not open CBO's own report (cbo.gov returned a script-only page), so this is a secondary relay.

statement: A Boston College retirement research brief finds a Social Security caregiver credit that replaces missing earnings with half the average wage index for up to five years would raise annual benefits by $1,172 a year for a caregiver after retirement.
anchor: This proposal typically involves replacing a person’s missing earnings with a credit equal to half of the average wage index for up to five years
This difference in annual benefits for receiving credit for up to five years is $1,172 a year
locator: Social Security Caregiver Credit section, p. 6
context: Center for Retirement Research at Boston College, December 2024, a back-of-the-envelope calculation for one caregiver, not a count of how many people a credit reaches (I found no Bipartisan Policy Center or Urban count). The brief also says the credit has no value to caregivers who are already retired or not working.

statement: In the legacy child-poverty model, the expanded-credit design (FAM-1A) with 400,000 voucher awards leaves child SPM poverty at 10.29%, 10.03% or 9.87% under moderate, enhanced or full delivery, with deep poverty at 2.28%, 2.19% or 2.13%.
context: Legacy model report (family-comparison-model-checks.md), a static source-year experiment; re-run with identical results on the official Census archive, November 12, 2026. Legacy project text (before October 28, 2026); a project estimate or record, not an outside score.

statement: In the legacy model, the units of children in deep poverty receive about $527 of existing credit on average, against an additional statutory credit of about $6,574 under the American Family Act analogue, in 2025 dollars before receipt assumptions.
anchor: source-deep-poor children's units have an average additional statutory credit of about $6,574 in 2025 dollars before receipt assumptions, compared with about $527 of existing unit credit.
